sens: Moral excellence, quality of one who acts rightly
Divine power, manifestation of God's strength
Admirable qualities that attract esteem and praise
G0703.detail:
1. Virtue is moral excellence, the quality of one who acts justly and rightly. It is what deserves approval and praise. In 2 Peter 1:5, Paul invites Christians to add virtue to their faith, as a quality to cultivate and develop in their lives.

2. Virtue can also refer to divine power itself, its manifested strength. In 2 Peter 1:3, God's "virtue" is what has given us everything pertaining to life and godliness — it is His working power.

3. Virtues are also the admirable and glorious qualities that deserve praise and recognition. In 1 Peter 2:9, Christians are called to proclaim the "virtues" of Him who called them out of darkness into His marvelous light — in other words, the splendid works and excellent qualities of God. The word evokes both excellence and the impression it produces on those who see it.
G0703.origine: The Greek word aretē comes from an ancient root meaning "that which shines, that which stands out." In ancient Greece, it initially referred to any form of remarkable superiority or outstanding advantage. Among Greek philosophers, it specialized in describing moral excellence. In the Septuagint, it translates the Hebrew hôd (glory, honor) and téhillâ (praise, glory), showing how the biblical word unites the idea of moral quality with that of public recognition.
G0703.emploi: The word aretē appears only 4 times in the New Testament, always in the epistles. In Philippians 4:8, it refers to the moral qualities that Christians should cultivate in their thoughts — the excellence of life that deserves approval. In 2 Peter 1:3 and 1:5, it becomes an element of spiritual progression: first the divine power that gives us life, then the virtue we must add to our faith as a personal effort. In 1 Peter 2:9, the context is more liturgical: proclaiming the virtues of God means declaring His mighty deeds and excellence. The biblical usage retains the idea that virtue is both an objective reality (goodness, power) and something that manifests outwardly and produces an impression of greatness.
G0703.portee: This word reminds us that virtue is not a human invention, but a participation in divine excellence. For the Christian, cultivating virtue means reflecting the qualities of God Himself, and this excellence of life becomes a silent testimony before others. Virtue is not a purely moral or philosophical virtue: it is rooted in the power and glory of God, and it must shine through our thoughts and actions for the praise of Him who saved us.

sens: Young of the sheep
Animal destined for sacrifice
Symbol of gentleness and vulnerability
G0704.detail:
1. The lamb is the young of the sheep, a domesticated animal raised by shepherds in the Middle East. It is a gentle and defenseless animal, completely dependent on its mother and the care of the shepherd.
2. In biblical tradition, the lamb is the quintessential sacrificial animal: it was offered as a burnt offering at the temple, especially during Passover (the Passover lamb), to obtain forgiveness of sins. This is why the word carries a strong religious connotation.
3. Jesus uses the word figuratively in Luke 10:3: "Behold, I send you out as lambs among wolves." The disciples are lambs — innocent, unarmed, vulnerable — sent into a hostile world. The image evokes the absence of earthly power and dependence on God.
G0704.origine: The Greek word arēn comes from roots that denote the sheep (likely related to arni, "lamb"). In ancient Hebrew, the words meryā' and kebes also referred to the lamb, particularly the male destined for sacrifice. The Greek word primarily appears in the earliest texts of the New Testament and translates these Hebrew terms in the Greek Bible of the Old Testament.
G0704.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 10:3, in the context where Jesus sends His disciples on a mission: "Go; behold, I send you out as lambs among wolves." Jesus warns them: they will encounter opposition and persecution. The contrast between the lamb (gentle, harmless) and the wolf (predator, violent) highlights the asymmetry of danger: the disciples should not expect to triumph by force, but to witness in vulnerability and rely on divine protection.
G0704.portee: For the Christian, this word teaches that the mission of the Church is not accomplished through political or military power, but in innocence, non-violence, and trust in God. It also invites acceptance of the sufferings and rejections that may accompany witnessing, not as a defeat, but as the normal path of the disciple — a path of lamb, not of conqueror.

sens: Enumerate the elements of a set to know the total number
Count a multitude to assess its size
Take into account, regard as worthy of interest or value
G0705.detail:
1. To count means to enumerate, to calculate the number of things or people: it is to mentally or materially add up what exists. Jesus says that even the hairs of our head are counted (Matthew 10:30, Luke 12:7): God knows them exactly, He loses nothing from view.
2. To enumerate is to establish the number of a multitude, especially a large one. In Revelation 7:9, a crowd so immense that no one could count it appears before the throne: the number exceeds anyone's ability to enumerate.
3. By extension, to count someone means to estimate them, to consider them as having value. When God counts every hair on your head, it signifies that He gives you extreme and personal attention.
G0705.origine: The word comes from the Greek root arithm- (arith-, number), which we recognize in the French "arithmétique." In Hebrew, this verb primarily renders סָפַר (sāpar), which also means to count or enumerate. The initial image is that of numeration: pointing out each element to accumulate the count.
G0705.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the New Testament, always in a context of divine knowledge or quantitative evaluation. Matthew and Luke, reporting the same teaching of Jesus, use "count" to affirm that God knows the smallest details of our lives: there is a link between enumerating and valuing. In Revelation 7:9, "counting" becomes impossible in the face of the multitude of the saved, illustrating human incapacity to measure divine redemption.
G0705.portee: This word reveals God's meticulous attention: nothing in our existence goes unnoticed, even the smallest details. This truth is not meant to instill fear, but to reassure: if God counts even the hairs on your head, it is to tell you that you matter to Him, that you are precious and watched over with love. It is a source of confidence when we feel lost or forgotten.

sens: Total quantity of elements or people that can be counted
Group or community considered by its size
Numerical value, figure
Importance or magnitude of a multitude
G0706.detail:
1. The primary meaning is everything that can be counted: a determined quantity of objects or people. Luke 22:3 mentions Judas as part of the "number of the twelve" apostles: the twelve are counted, and Judas is one of them.
2. By extension, the "number" designates the entirety of a group considered in its quantitative aspect. Acts 4:4 states that "the number of men grew to about five thousand": it is the entire community of believers that is being measured. Acts 6:7 speaks of a Church whose "number of disciples was increasing greatly".
3. On a concrete and practical level, it is the act of counting or the result: Revelation 9:16 refers to "the number of the horsemen of the army", meaning a quantity so enormous that it impresses by its vastness.
4. In a more figurative or symbolic manner, especially in Revelation, the number takes on a significance of a sign or mysterious magnitude: Revelation 13:17-18 assigns a "number" to the name of the beast, suggesting a riddle or a secret hidden in the numbers.
G0706.origine: The Greek word arithmos comes from an ancient root meaning "to count" or "to arrange in order". It appears in classical Greek in the sense of "number" or "quantity". In the Greek Old Testament, it generally translates the Hebrew "mispar", which has the same concrete meaning of counting or headcount. This word belongs to the family of elementary mathematical concepts that any ancient reader would have understood: counting livestock, warriors, the faithful.
G0706.emploi: The word "number" appears about fifteen times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts and Revelation. In Acts, it almost always describes the growth of disciples or believers: in Jerusalem (Acts 4:4, 6:7), in the villages (Acts 16:5). It is a sign of divine blessing and the success of the Gospel. In Revelation, its usage changes: numbers often become enormous (myriads of myriads, Revelation 5:11, 9:16) or symbolic (the number of the beast, Revelation 13:17-18, or the 144,000, Revelation 7:4). This distinction shows how the word shifts from the concrete (counting the converts) to the mysterious (the numerical riddles of the end times).
G0706.portee: For the believer, the increasing "numbers" in Acts remind us that the Church grows by the power of the Holy Spirit, not by human strength. In Revelation, the symbolic numbers invite meditation on the secrets of God and His absolute mastery: even the countless myriads are known to Him who sits on the throne. This word teaches us that God never loses sight of detail, from the smallest group to the crowds that surpass understanding.

sens: City in Palestine from which Joseph originated
Location probably situated in Judea, in a mountainous region
G0707.detail:
1. Arimathea is a small city in Palestine, primarily known as the hometown of Joseph, the rich man who asked Pilate for the body of Jesus to bury Him (Matthew 27:57; Mark 15:43). It is an ordinary place, without political significance, but it becomes famous due to this act of piety towards Jesus.

2. According to Luke 23:51, Arimathea is described as a "city of the Jews", which simply specifies its location in Judea. Its Hebrew name likely means "height" or "hill" (Rama), which may correspond to its geographical situation in a mountainous region of Palestine.
G0707.origine: The Greek name Arimathaia transliterates the Hebrew word Rama or Ramataim, which means "height" or "hills". It was a small locality in Judea, also mentioned in the Old Testament (1 Samuel 1:1) as the land of Elkanah, the father of the prophet Samuel. The same place bears different forms of the same name according to the texts and languages.
G0707.emploi: Arimathea appears four times in the New Testament, always in connection with Joseph who was from there. Matthew (27:57), Mark (15:43), Luke (23:51), and John (19:38) all mention "Joseph of Arimathea". Luke adds that he was a distinguished "counselor" (probably a member of the Sanhedrin), and that this city was in Judea. John specifies that Joseph was a secret disciple of Jesus, for fear of the Jewish authorities. This name appears only in the context of the passion and burial of the Lord.

sens: Travel companion of the apostle Paul from Thessalonica
Man who traveled with Paul in Asia and to Jerusalem
Prisoner who accompanied Paul on his journey to Rome
Collaborator of Paul in the missionary work
G0708.detail:
1. Aristarchus is a Macedonian from Thessalonica who meets Paul in Ephesus (Acts 19:29). He is part of Paul's group of travelers and is even caught up in the confusion at the theater of Ephesus during the silversmiths' riot against the disciples.

2. He accompanies Paul on his journey through Asia towards Jerusalem: Paul takes him with him to return to Asia, alongside other companions like Sopater, Secundus, and Timothy (Acts 20:4).

3. Later, Aristarchus travels with Paul on the ship heading to Asia, still described as a Macedonian from Thessalonica (Acts 27:2), which shows this man's lasting loyalty to Paul.

4. Paul calls Aristarchus his "fellow prisoner" in the letter to the Colossians (Colossians 4:10), indicating that he shared Paul's imprisonment, probably in Rome. He is also mentioned among Paul's fellow workers in the letter to Philemon (Philemon 1:24).
G0708.origine: The Greek name Aristarchus literally means "one who rules best" or "excellent leader" (from "aristos" = best, and "archos" = leader). It is a typically Greek name that reflects the aristocratic values of ancient Greece. The character bears this honorable name as a simple designation among Paul's companions.
G0708.emploi: Aristarchus appears five times in the New Testament, exclusively in Paul's writings. He is first introduced as a Macedonian from Thessalonica met in Ephesus (Acts 19:29), then listed among the companions accompanying Paul on his missionary journeys (Acts 20:4 and 27:2). These last two references show that Paul held him in high regard and regularly included him in his travels. In the epistles, Paul refers to him as his "fellow prisoner" (Colossians 4:10), meaning that Aristarchus shared the apostle's imprisonment, likely during his stay in Rome. Finally, Philemon 1:24 names him among Paul's "fellow workers", highlighting his active role in the apostolic ministry.
G0708.portee: Aristarchus embodies faithfulness and dedication to the cause of the Gospel. His example shows a disciple who does not settle for mere adherence to the faith but who accepts to travel with Paul despite dangers, and even to share his captivity. For the Christian reader, Aristarchus reminds us that serving Christ may require leaving one's homeland, following the apostles on their journeys, and persevering through trials.

sens: To have a morning meal, breakfast
To have a meal in general, to eat
G0709.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to have a meal in the early morning, before starting work. This is what the disciples do with the resurrected Jesus when he invites them: "Come, eat" (John 21:12), as it is early morning by the Sea of Tiberias. The word comes from "aristos," which refers to this first nourishing meal of the day.
2. Over time, in common Greek, the word broadens and can simply mean "to have a meal" at any time. A Pharisee invites Jesus to "dine" at his home (Luke 11:37), which shows that the word now describes the general act of eating together, without time restrictions.
G0709.origine: The word comes from the name "aristos" which designates the morning meal, breakfast — the time when one was hungry after a night of work. This meal was considered an important part of the ancient day. The word retains this root to name the action of eating, even when its meaning has broadened to include other meals over time.
G0709.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament. Twice in the Gospel of John (21:12 and 21:15) during the appearance of the resurrected Jesus by the lake, where he invites his disciples to eat: the morning context of breakfast is clear. Once in Luke (11:37), when a Pharisee invites Jesus to dine at his home — here the word has lost its morning specificity and simply denotes a meal of hospitality. This evolution from a specific meal (breakfast) to any meal shows how living language broadens the meanings of words.
G0709.portee: This simple verb reminds us that in the Gospels, shared meals are key moments of communion: the resurrected Jesus eats with his disciples to show that he is truly alive, and invitations to eat open doors to the word. Eating together is never trivial: it is always an occasion for relationship.

sens: Left side of the body or space, as opposed to the right
Lower or less honorable position
Weapon or shield intended for defense
G0710.detail: 1. The word simply designates the left side, whether it is a part of the body (the left hand in Matthew 6:3) or a position in space (to the left of the place of crucifixion in Luke 23:33). It is the opposite of "right" in the sense of direction. 2. In ancient cultures, the left was generally associated with what is inferior or less honorable, while the right symbolized prestige and power; thus, sitting on the left was less prestigious than sitting on the right (Mark 10:37). 3. In 2 Corinthians 6:7, the word describes the defensive weapons of righteousness — the shield that the soldier holds on his left to protect himself — as opposed to offensive weapons.
G0710.origine: The word comes from a Greek root evoking the idea of direction or side. In Hebrew, we find שְׂמֹאול (semôl), which has the same meaning. Greek does not have a known specific older term; this word belongs to the common vocabulary of spatial localization and body description.
G0710.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, mainly in spatial and bodily contexts. In Matthew and Mark, it indicates a physical position: Matthew uses it for the left hand (symbol of discreet action), Mark for a position of relative prestige next to the Lord. In Luke, it locates one of the two criminals on the cross. In 2 Corinthians, Paul transfers the word to the military and spiritual domain, applying it to the defenses of the Christian. The meaning remains literal and concrete in all cases.
G0710.portee: This word reminds us that ordinary gestures — including those of the left hand — should not be forgotten or neglected. It also teaches us that what the world considers an inferior position (the left) is not a disgrace: in the Kingdom of God, places of honor are distributed according to the Father's will, not according to our ambitions. Finally, in a spiritual military context, it emphasizes that the defense of our soul — its protection — is as important as the attack against evil.

sens: Christian from Rome known to the apostle Paul
G0711.detail: Aristobulus is a Christian mentioned by Paul in his letter to the Romans. Paul greets him as well as the members of his household, indicating that Aristobulus was known for his faith and likely played a role in the Christian community of Rome in the 1st century.
G0711.origine: The name Aristobulus comes from Greek and literally means "of the best counsel" or "excellent advisor" (from ἄριστος, "excellent," and βουλή, "counsel"). It is a common Greek name among educated members of Roman and Jewish society in the 1st century.
G0711.emploi: Aristobulus is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Romans 16:10, where Paul includes him in his final greetings to the Church in Rome. The fact that Paul specifically greets "those of the household of Aristobulus" suggests that he was a person of respectable social status, capable of hosting Christians and accompanying them in their faith. This mention shows that by the mid-1st century, the Gospel had reached the educated and well-established circles of Rome.
G0711.portee: The mention of Aristobulus reminds the reader that the early Christian faith was not limited to the poor or marginalized, but also reached people of high social rank. It is an invitation to recognize that the Gospel addresses all walks of life and creates a fraternal community where human distinctions fade away.

sens: Originally, breakfast or the morning meal
In a broader sense, any meal, particularly an important meal or reception
A feast or banquet to which guests are invited
G0712.detail:
1. The word primarily designates breakfast, the meal taken in the morning in ancient Greece. This is its proper and original meaning.
2. In the later Greek of the New Testament, it has taken on a broader meaning and simply denotes a meal, without specifying the time. This is seen in Luke 11:38: the Pharisee notes that Jesus did not wash before the meal, without particular distinction.
3. The word can also evoke a solemn meal, a feast where guests are received. In Matthew 22:4, the king prepares a great feast for the wedding of his son and sends to call the guests — it is an important event, not just a simple daily meal.
4. Similarly, in Luke 14:12, when one gives a dinner or supper and invites guests, it implies a meal of some significance, not just a simple snack.
G0712.origine: The Greek word ἄριστον comes from a root that refers to the idea of what is excellent or first. Its original meaning in classical Greek is "breakfast" or "morning meal" (literally, "the first meal"), as the Greeks began their day with this meal. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew word לֶחֶם (lekhem), which simply means "bread" or "food." By the time of the New Testament, as in later Greek, the word had broadened its meaning and could denote any important meal.
G0712.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament (Matthew 22:4, Luke 11:38, Luke 14:12), always in contexts of ordinary meals or receptions. In Matthew 22:4, it describes the feast prepared for the wedding of the king's son: it is a festive and solemn event. In Luke 11:38, the Pharisee is surprised that Jesus did not wash before the meal, which shows that the word here denotes the meal of the day, without major particularity. In Luke 14:12, Jesus speaks of giving a dinner or supper, a meal where guests are invited — again, it is a meal of social importance. The word does not carry any particular theological weight; it is a practical and concrete term.
G0712.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of meals in biblical life: they are not only a physical necessity but occasions for communion, hospitality, and sharing. Jesus uses the meal as an image of a restored relationship or a coming judgment (the parable of the wedding feast in Matthew 22). It is also a place where charity is expressed: whom do we invite to the table, and for what reasons?

sens: To be sufficient for a need, a given situation
To be enough, to meet what is required
G0713.detail:
1. The word expresses that something is enough, that it fully meets a need or a requirement of the moment. In Matthew 6:34, Jesus says: "Sufficient for the day is its own trouble" — meaning that the difficulties of a day are already ample enough in themselves, without us worrying about tomorrow. The word describes a perfect adequacy: what is present is exactly what is needed.
2. The word can also mean "to be enough" in the sense of "it is enough that…", marking a limit or equality. In Matthew 10:25, Jesus states: "It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher" — in other words, the disciple should not expect better than what his teacher has received; that is sufficient for him. In 1 Peter 4:3, "it is enough to have done the will of the Gentiles", the word means that it is not necessary to continue down that path: enough has been done in that way.
G0713.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb ἀρκέω, which literally means "to repel, to ward off" — an image of one who stands firm or pushes forward — then "to suffice, to be enough". The basic idea is that of a force or provision that repels lack, that wards off scarcity. The word belongs to the family of Greek terms expressing self-sufficiency and satisfaction.
G0713.emploi: This word appears three times in the New Testament, always with the meaning of "to suffice" or "to be enough". In Matthew 6:34 and 10:25, it is used in the neutral state to express an objective sufficiency — what is present is sufficient. In 1 Peter 4:3, it introduces an exhortation: it is enough to have acted that way in the past; now, it is finished. The context is always that of a healthy limitation, an acceptance of what is given or what has been, without excess or unnecessary regret.
G0713.portee: This word speaks directly to the Christian's trust: it invites not to burden oneself with worry for the future (Matthew 6:34), to accept to share in Christ's fate without murmuring (Matthew 10:25), and to resolutely turn away from a previous life of sin (1 Peter 4:3). "Suffice" reminds us that God provides for the present and that the past should no longer chain us.

sens: To have enough strength or resources to meet a need
To be satisfied, to be content with what one has
G0714.detail:
1. The verb expresses the idea that a thing, a quantity, or help is sufficient to accomplish something or meet a necessity. It is to have enough. When Philip asks for bread to feed the crowd, he says that two hundred denarii would not suffice (John 6:7): the amount is not large enough. Or when Paul says that God's grace is sufficient for him (2 Corinthians 12:9), it means that this grace has enough power to support his weakness.
2. The verb can also mean to be satisfied, to be content, not to ask for more. When Jesus tells the soldiers to be content with their wages (Luke 3:14), he asks them to find sufficient what they receive and to stop demanding more. It is a call to inner satisfaction. Similarly, if we have food and clothing, that should be enough for us (1 Timothy 6:8): we must be content with that.
G0714.origine: The verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of holding firm, resisting, or helping. The primary meaning was probably to help someone or support them. From this core, the idea of having enough strength or means to support, thus to suffice, emerged. The notion of satisfaction naturally follows: if something meets my needs, I am satisfied.
G0714.emploi: The word appears eight times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and the epistles. It is always used to express that a quantity, help, or grace is large enough to meet a need. Sometimes it is used impersonally ("it is enough"), sometimes with a dative indicating the satisfied person. Its use varies: in the narratives, it denotes material insufficiency (bread, money); in the words of Jesus and Paul, it evokes spiritual sufficiency (grace, the presence of the Father). It is a word from the realm of daily economy and trust in God.
G0714.portee: This word invites the reader to understand that God always gives enough, and that true wealth consists in being content with what He provides. It calls for both realism (recognizing material limits) and faith (trusting that grace is sufficient). It is a word of liberation: one who is content with little is neither a slave to greed nor anxiety.

sens: Large terrestrial animal with thick fur, carnivorous and powerful
G0715.detail: 1. The bear is a well-known wild creature in the Mediterranean world and ancient Middle East, feared for its strength and size. The word designates this animal in all its physical breadth, particularly its imposing body structure. In Revelation 13:2, the bear appears in the symbolic vision of the beast: its feet "like those of a bear" evoke the brute and threatening power of this eschatological creature, associated with the pagan empires that oppose the people of God.
G0715.origine: The Greek word ἄρκτος comes from an Indo-European root designating wild and powerful animals. The Hebrew דֹּב (dov) corresponds exactly to this same animal in the Greek Old Testament. The word does not have a significant lexical family in Greek, as it directly designates a well-defined creature, without common metaphorical derivatives.
G0715.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in John's apocalyptic vision (Revelation 13:2). The apostle composes the image of the eschatological beast by assembling traits of fearsome animals: head of a leopard, feet of a bear, mouth of a lion. Each animal symbolizes a characteristic of hostile power: the bear brings the idea of brute force and crushing. This image recalls an Old Testament symbolism where animals embody empires (Daniel 7).
G0715.portee: For the reader, the bear in this passage conveys the physical and military threat: it represents the earthly power that crushes under its weight. But John reminds us that this beast, despite its apparent terror, derives its authority only from the fallen dragon and remains subject to divine judgment. This word invites the Christian not to fear the violence of empires, since the Lord remains their master.

sens: Vehicle drawn by horses, mounted on two wheels and without a roof
Imaginary or symbolic structure likened to a chariot in a vision
G0716.detail:
1. A chariot is a two-wheeled vehicle drawn by horses, without a roof or enclosed body: it was the means of transport for high-ranking individuals and warriors in antiquity. The Ethiopian eunuch in Acts 8:28 "was returning, sitting in his chariot, and reading the prophet Isaiah" — this is how an important person traveled, comfortably enough to read along the way. Philip runs to this chariot (Acts 8:29) to join the traveler, and both descend into the water for baptism (Acts 8:38).
2. In apocalyptic visions, "chariot" refers to a heavenly or hellish reality: in Revelation 9:9, the creatures seen by John produce "the sound of chariots with many horses rushing into battle," an image of the tumult and destructive power of the final plagues.
G0716.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "to join, assemble" — a chariot is a device where all the parts are joined together. The Greek Bible uses it to translate the Hebrew word "rekeb" (mount, war chariot, or parade chariot). It is a concrete and common word in the ancient world, where the chariot was a valuable asset.
G0716.emploi: The word "chariot" appears only four times in the New Testament. Three occurrences are concentrated in the same passage: Acts 8:28-38, where the account of the Ethiopian eunuch's baptism revolves entirely around the chariot as a setting and narrative stake — it is the context of Philip's mission. A single occurrence in Revelation 9:9 is figurative, in a vision where the chariots evoke an innumerable army and the terrifying sound of war. The word retains the same basic meaning everywhere: a horse-drawn vehicle.
G0716.portee: For the ancient reader, the chariot symbolizes prestige and material resources. In Acts 8, it is by getting into the chariot of a wealthy and influential stranger that Philip announces to this man the Good News of Christ — a powerful image that the Spirit crosses all social barriers to reach even the powerful. In Revelation, the sound of the chariots reminds that the final judgment will be powerful and relentless.

sens: Place where the final great eschatological battle is to take place
G0717.detail: Armageddon is a place whose Hebrew name means "mountain of Megiddo." Megiddo was a fortified city in ancient Israel, famous for several historical battles (notably that of King Josiah reported in 2 Chronicles 35:22). In Revelation, John uses this historical place name as a symbol of the final battle between good and evil, where God will gather the nations before the final judgment (Revelation 16:16).
G0717.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew הַר מְגִדּוֹן (har megiddôn), literally "mountain of Megiddo." הַר means "mountain" and Megiddo was a fortified city in Galilee, strategically important in the Old Testament. John takes this historically charged geographical name to make it a prophetic symbol of the place of the final battle.
G0717.emploi: Armageddon appears only once in the Bible, in Revelation 16:16. John reports that the contents of the three bowls of plagues are poured out, and demonic spirits gather the kings of the earth in this place called Armageddon in Hebrew. This is the setting that John establishes for the events of the end times, without describing it in detail elsewhere.
G0717.portee: Armageddon reminds the reader that God is in control of history and the outcome of things. Even when evil seems to triumph and nations unite against good, it is God who gathers them for judgment. This historical name turned prophetic invites unwavering trust in divine sovereignty and spiritual vigilance in the face of the approaching last days.

sens: To unite two people by a promise of marriage
To solemnly engage the Church to Christ
G0718.detail:
1. In the concrete sense, it is to establish a marriage bond between two people, or more precisely to solemnly promise that they will marry: a commitment, a firm promise is established between them. This is what is called engagement.
2. In a figurative and theological sense, Paul uses this word to say that he has engaged the Church of the Corinthians to become the bride of Christ, presenting her to him as a faithful and pure virgin (2 Corinthians 11:2). The spiritual marriage has not yet been celebrated — it is a solemn promise that binds the Church to her Lord.
G0718.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to adapt, join, make correspond." It is the idea of adjusting two things together to make one. Applied to marriage, it is to unite two people, to "adapt" them to each other. This Greek word translates the Hebrew אמן (aman) in the Old Testament, which evokes the idea of entrusting and holding firm.
G0718.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Paul's letter to the Corinthians. Paul uses it to express his apostolic role: like a father or a close friend, he has solemnly engaged the Church to belong to Christ, her only husband. It is a figurative and poetic use of the word, which emphasizes both the irrevocable commitment and the purity required of the Church. The context shows that Paul fears this spiritual engagement may be compromised — that the Church may turn away from Christ to false doctrines (2 Corinthians 11:2-4).
G0718.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the Church is not a mere organization, but the fiancée of Christ — bound to him by a solemn and sacred promise. She must maintain purity and fidelity to her Lord until the eternal marriage in heaven. It is a call to moral and doctrinal consistency, and a comfort: the bond that attaches us to Christ is as secure and precious as a marriage promise.

sens: Articulation point where two bones or two parts meet and unite
Intimate and secret union between two spiritual or immaterial elements
G0719.detail:
1. The joint is primarily the place where two bones join to allow movement of the body. In Hebrews 4:12, the word of God penetrates "to the dividing of soul and spirit, joints and marrow": it reaches the deepest structures of our being, beyond what is visible, even to the intimate joints that unite the different dimensions of our spiritual existence.

2. By extension, a joint refers to anything that binds and unites two realities together, like a secret or hidden articulation. In this biblical context, it evokes the mysterious union between the soul (emotional and psychological life) and the spirit (spiritual dimension) — a union that only the word of God can scrutinize and separate.
G0719.origine: The Greek word harmos comes from a root meaning "to fit together," "to assemble," "to join together." It originally denotes the action and result of putting two things in close contact so that they function as a whole. In Hebrew, the corresponding word is generally "pesaḥ" or terms related to the joints of the human body. The same Greek root has produced other words related to assembly and harmony.
G0719.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 4:12. This unique usage makes it a particularly precise and chosen term to express the penetrating effectiveness of the word of God. The author of the letter to the Hebrews uses it to show that the divine word does not stop at the surface of our being: it crosses all natural boundaries — those between soul and spirit, between bones and marrow — and even reaches the joints, that is, the most intimate points of union where the immaterial realities of our existence are tied together.
G0719.portee: This word reminds the reader that God does not only judge our outward acts, but he knows and discerns the deepest intimacy of our heart and spirit. The word of God acts like a mirror that exposes our hidden thoughts and feelings, even to the very joints of our inner life. It is both a warning against hypocrisy and an invitation to transparency before God.

sens: to say no, refuse to acknowledge a truth
to reject someone, refuse to admit or support them
to renounce something, to turn away from it through one's actions
G0720.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: to say "no," to refuse to admit or acknowledge something. Peter does this in Matthew 26:70 when he claims not to know Jesus; John the Baptist does this in John 1:20 by denying that he is the Christ — he uses this word to clarify what he is not.

2. A more serious meaning: to renounce someone is to disavow them, to refuse to acknowledge them as someone of value or importance. Acts 3:13 speaks of the Jews who renounced Jesus before Pilate — they rejected him, refusing to acknowledge him as worthy of life.

3. To deny a spiritual or moral reality through one's behavior: in 1 Timothy 5:8, not caring for one's own is to deny the faith — one acts as if faith does not exist or does not matter. This is a denial in actions, not just in words.
G0720.origine: The Greek word ἀρνέομαι comes from a root that means to say "no" or refuse. In ancient Hebrew, the verb כָּחַשׁ (kachash) expresses the idea of refusing or denying — the same sense of rejection. This verb belongs to the family of words related to negation and refusal in ancient Greek and in the Hebrew Bible.
G0720.emploi: The word appears 30 times in the New Testament, primarily in Matthew, Luke, and John, and in the epistles. Its usage carries three main nuances. First, the denial of truths or identities: Peter denies Jesus three times (Matthew 26:70, Luke 22:57, John 13:38); John the Baptist denies being the Christ (John 1:20). Next, personal rejection: the authorities of Jerusalem renounced Jesus (Acts 3:13, 3:14). Finally, ethical abandonment: denying the faith through one's behavior (1 Timothy 5:8), denying God through one's works (Titus 1:16). The word can carry a strong spiritual condemnation: Jesus warns that he will deny before the Father anyone who denies him before men (Matthew 10:33).
G0720.portee: This word invites the Christian to faithfulness and consistency. To deny Jesus is to reject him either in words, in actions, or by forgetting him in one's life. Jesus takes this denial very seriously: it has eternal consequences. For the believer, this does not mean that faith must be loud, but that it cannot be invisible or contradicted by behavior. It is a call to live according to what one confesses.

sens: Young sheep, innocent animal
Jesus Christ as the sacrificial victim, given for the sins of the world
The glorified Bridegroom in the marriage of the Church
The risen and triumphant Lord who reigns over all things
The one worthy of praise, honor, and eternal glory
G0721.detail:
1. The lamb is primarily a young sheep, a symbol of weakness and innocence: Jesus says to Peter, "Feed my lambs" (John 21:15), referring to the young Christians entrusted to him, gentle and vulnerable like young sheep.

2. In the biblical context, the lamb especially evokes the victim of sacrifice: Revelation speaks of "the lamb that was slain" (Revelation 13:8), designating Jesus offered as a sacrificial victim for the sins of the world, fulfilling the Passover sacrifice of the Old Testament.

3. Revelation also presents the lamb as a glorified bridegroom: "Blessed are those who are called to the marriage supper of the lamb" (Revelation 19:9), an image of the intimate and eternal union of Christ with his Church.

4. The word finally designates the risen and triumphant Christ who reigns over the universe: "all will worship him" (Revelation 13:8), and he is worthy that "all creatures" give him glory (Revelation 5:13).

5. The lamb is the one to whom the book of life belongs, the one who opens the seals of divine judgment, the one whose name is written in heaven — in summary, the supreme Lord worthy of all honor and power forever and ever.
G0721.origine: The Greek word ἀρνίον is a diminutive (diminutive form) of the word ἀρήν, which simply means "ram" or "sheep." This diminutive emphasizes smallness and tenderness: a little lamb, a young and fragile creature. In Hebrew, the Old Testament speaks of the Passover lamb (כֶּבֶשׂ, kevesh), and the Greek translation of the Old Testament uses this word to refer to lamb sacrifices. The diminutive arnion in the New Testament, particularly in John and Revelation, enriches the image: Jesus is not only a victim, he is the one who takes upon himself weakness and vulnerability to save his people.
G0721.emploi: The word appears 28 times in the New Testament, primarily in Revelation (27 occurrences) and once in John. John 21:15 uses it literally: Peter must feed the lambs, meaning the young disciples entrusted to his care. But from Revelation 5:6 onward, the context becomes clearly Christological: John sees a "slain" lamb in heaven, an image of the sacrificed Christ. From there, all of Revelation is structured around this triumphant lamb: he is the one who opens the seals of judgment (Revelation 6:1), whose name is written in the book of life (Revelation 13:8), who welcomes the martyrs and the virgins (Revelation 14:1-4), and who reigns eternally in the heavenly Jerusalem (Revelation 21:22-23). The lamb embodies both the offered Redeemer and the glorified King, the Savior and the Judge — two inseparable aspects of the mystery of Christ.
G0721.portee: This word invites the Christian to contemplate the heart of the faith: Jesus offered himself as an innocent lamb to take away the sins of the world (implicit reference to John 1:29). But there is not only a past sacrifice — the lamb is also alive, resurrected, in heaven, worthy of eternal glory and the object of the praise of all creation. For the believer, it is a call to worship and trust: the same Christ who humbled himself to death now reigns with power. It is also a word of tenderness addressed to the disciples: we are his lambs, small, fragile, but kept and loved by the one who gave his life for us.

sens: To turn the soil with a plow or agricultural tool
To cultivate the land, prepare the soil for sowing
To work hard at a useful and productive task
G0722.detail: 1. To plow primarily means to turn the soil using a plow or agricultural tool to prepare it to receive seeds (Luke 17:7, where the master asks the servant returning from the fields to come and sit at the table after having plowed). 2. It is also the general action of cultivating the land, this essential and perpetual work that allows for the nourishment of people. 3. Figuratively, the word evokes any serious and productive work: in 1 Corinthians 9:10, Paul uses it to show that the one who plows has the right to a share of the fruit of their labor, thus applying the image of the plowman to the preacher of the Gospel who must carry out their ministry with confidence in the promised reward.
G0722.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek ἄροτρον (arotron), the plow itself. It is a more recent form of the verb ἀρόω (aroō), which means the same thing. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this verb translates the Hebrew חָרַשׁ (harash, to plow) and occasionally עֲדַר (adar, to pasture). The word refers to a fundamental reality of Mediterranean agrarian life: the plow drawn by animals, essential for transforming barren soil into fertile fields.
G0722.emploi: The verb appears twice in the New Testament. In Luke 17:7, Jesus uses it in a parable about service: a master does not ask his servant to rest immediately after plowing, but to serve him at the table. The context is one of obedience and duty without expecting recognition. In 1 Corinthians 9:10, Paul applies the word to apostolic work: he cites a principle drawn from the Law (the one who plows must do so with the hope of sharing in it) to justify that preachers have the right to live from their ministry. In both cases, plowing is a legitimate, fundamental work, and worthy of remuneration.
G0722.portee: This word reminds the reader that honest and productive work has biblical dignity: it is not a curse, but a necessity of life and a participation in the order of creation. For the believer, it also invites one to see in all Christian work — in preaching, teaching, serving — an activity comparable to plowing: it requires perseverance, promises a harvest, and those who dedicate themselves to it have the right to live from it with dignity.

sens: Agricultural tool used to till the soil
The act of plowing or cultivating the ground
Total commitment to a task, with no turning back
G0723.detail:
1. The plow is the tool that the farmer pulls to turn over and prepare the soil before sowing. It is a heavy and essential instrument for agricultural work (Luke 9:62).
2. To put one's hand to the plow means to engage in the work of tilling, symbolizing the regular and laborious work required for cultivating the land.
3. Figuratively, "putting one's hand to the plow" becomes the image of a wholehearted commitment to the service of God: whoever looks back is not fully devoted to this task (Luke 9:62).
G0723.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb ἀρόω which means "to plow." It is a concrete and common term designating the fundamental tool of Mediterranean agriculture. In Hebrew, the corresponding word is עֵת (a concrete form of plowing).
G0723.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 9:62, where Jesus uses it to reject an insufficient application for discipleship. One of the applicants wanted to first say goodbye to his family, but Jesus shows that following the Kingdom of God requires a total and irreversible decision, like that of the plowman who must not look back while walking straight in his furrow.
G0723.portee: This image of the plowman reminds the Christian that the commitment to Jesus is total and uncompromising. Looking back — that is, regretting the past, hesitating between two worlds, or wanting to keep one foot behind — disqualifies the disciple. The plow symbolizes the necessity of a singular focus and unwavering determination in faith.

sens: The act of appropriating someone else's property by violence or coercion
Loot, stolen goods or obtained by force
Figuratively: dishonest enrichment, extortion
Dispossession, loss of property suffered by force
G0724.detail:
1. Robbery is the act of taking by violence what belongs to someone else — stealing brutally, stripping, extorting. It is a criminal act, not a mere discreet theft. Jesus reproaches the Pharisees for being "full of robbery" (Matthew 23:25), targeting their dishonest greed and exploitation of others.

2. The loot itself, what has been stolen or forcibly taken. Luke 11:39 reports the same criticism: the inside of the Pharisees is filled not only with robbery (the theft) but with wickedness, showing that their extortion practices reveal a corrupt heart.

3. In a broader sense, robbery refers to enrichment by dishonest means, systematic exploitation. The word conveys a mentality of greed and theft, not just isolated acts.

4. In Hebrews 10:34, the word takes on the meaning of loss or dispossession: Christians "joyfully accepted the plundering of your goods," meaning that their possessions were forcibly taken from them (during persecutions), and they endured it with courage because they knew they had "better and lasting possessions."
G0724.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb ἁρπάζω (harpazô), which means "to seize," "to snatch away," "to take by force." The basic image is that of a hand gripping, tearing away. The word has the same root as the notion of violent removal. In ancient Hebrew, terms like גָּזֵל (gazal, "to steal") or similar conveyed the same idea of dispossession by force. It is always a pejorative term: there is no "good robbery."
G0724.emploi: The word appears only three times in the provided New Testament. Two occurrences are found in Jesus' parallel rebuke in Matthew 23:25 and Luke 11:39: he addresses the Pharisees and denounces their hypocrisy — they pretend to be outwardly pure but are inwardly full of robbery, that is, dishonest greed and exploitation. The third usage, Hebrews 10:34, shifts perspective slightly: it refers to the "plundering" of goods (the forced dispossession suffered by persecuted believers), not the act of seizing. In all cases, the word denotes a taking of property by force, either committed by the Pharisees or endured by the martyrs.
G0724.portee: For the Christian, this word first sheds light on Jesus' warning: holiness is not a matter of outward appearance, but of the heart. A superficial piety that hides greed and exploitation is serious hypocrisy. Furthermore, the courage of Hebrews 10:34 invites those suffering persecution to look beyond the material: losing one's goods here is not a true disaster if one possesses the eternal inheritance. The word reminds us that the desire for ill-gotten gains is incompatible with life in Christ.

sens: the act of seizing or taking by force
what is seized, loot or prey
possessed conquest that one keeps jealously
G0725.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the violent gesture of seizing something: the act of taking by force. It is a dynamic action, an aggressive movement.

2. It can also refer to the result of this action: what has been seized, what has become loot or prey. Psalm 22:25 (in the Greek version) uses it to speak of the prey torn away by a lion.

3. Figuratively, the word expresses a possession enjoyed as a personal conquest: something one has appropriated and refuses to lose. In Philippians 2:6, Paul uses it to describe a divine dignity that one clings to.
G0725.origine: The word comes from the verb "to seize" (harpazô), which evokes the visceral image of a hand that grabs and holds. The family includes "harpax" (one who steals, who takes away) and "harpage" (loot). In classical Greek, it is a word of violent and rapid action. In the Greek Old Testament, it often corresponds to the Hebrew "גָּזֵל" (to take away by force).
G0725.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 2:6, a crucial verse about the nature of Christ. Paul questions the relationship of the pre-existing Christ to his divine dignity: is it something he seized and would hold onto jealously, or rather a reality he never considered as a personal possession to defend? The context of this passage — where Paul describes the humiliation of Christ who emptied himself — suggests that the word evokes the idea of a grasping, a selfish appropriation of a position or power.
G0725.portee: This word invites the believer to meditate on the paradox of Christ: He who could have exercised his equality with God as a precious possession to preserve instead abandoned it out of love. It questions our own relationship to the advantages, powers, and rights we have: do we seize them selfishly, or do we put them at the service of love? This word helps to grasp the depth of the incarnation and the humility of the Savior.

sens: To grasp something or someone with violence and speed
To snatch, steal, openly rob
To carry away, to take suddenly
To take by force, to seize
To snatch or take away in a supernatural or spiritual sense
G0726.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a physical and violent action: to seize something with force and promptness, like a wolf that snatches sheep (John 10:12), or Herod who seizes John the Baptist. It is the gesture of a robber who steals.

2. The word also applies to abstract or precious things: the evil one takes away the word of the kingdom sown in the heart (Matthew 13:19), or the violent take the kingdom of heaven by force (Matthew 11:12)—not by brute force, but by a fervor that refuses to wait.

3. In the accounts of Acts, the word describes an urgent removal: Paul is taken away from the crowd that wants to lynch him (Acts 23:10), Philip is snatched away by the Spirit (Acts 8:39). It is the sudden movement of an authority that intervenes.

4. In eschatological passages, Paul describes believers being taken up to the Lord: "caught up to heaven" (Revelation 12:5), "caught up together" (1 Thessalonians 4:17). The word retains its dramatic force, but it becomes divine.

5. In Jude, it is the act of saving someone by snatching them from peril: snatching others from the fire (Jude 1:23), pulling them from danger urgently.
G0726.origine: The verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of seizing violently and carrying away. In Greek, the verb harpazō and the noun harpax ("snatcher") belong to the same family. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, this verb primarily translates the Hebrew gazal (to steal, to rob) and taraf (to tear, to snatch). The image is always that of a hand that grips and a force that carries away.
G0726.emploi: The verb appears 14 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew, John, and Paul. In the Gospels, it describes violent actions: the evil one who steals the word (Matthew 13:19), the wolf that snatches the sheep (John 10:12-29), the crowd that wants to take Jesus away (John 6:15). In Acts, it is a verb of urgency: Paul taken away from the crowd (Acts 23:10), Philip snatched away by the Spirit (Acts 8:39). In Paul, the word takes on a heavenly dimension: believers caught up to heaven (1 Thessalonians 4:17, 2 Corinthians 12:2-4). In Jude and Revelation, it retains its force to describe decisive, salvific, or divine actions.
G0726.portee: This verb teaches that the things of God are not taken lightly: it requires a fervent resolution and urgency to enter the kingdom (Matthew 11:12). It also shows that our security depends on the hand of the Father, powerful to keep us and to snatch us from evil (John 10:29, Jude 1:23). For the Christian, this word reminds us that salvation is not a lukewarm transaction, but a capture by divine grace.

sens: One who seizes, who takes away by force
One who steals, who plunders others
One who uses robbery, extortion
By extension: crook, scammer
G0727.detail:
1. The word first depicts the action of seizing or taking something away with violence. Jesus uses it to describe wolves that attack the sheep: it is the image of a predator capturing its prey (Matthew 7:15).
2. It designates one who steals or plunders: not just a stealthy theft, but an act of robbery where one takes what belongs to another by force or cunning. The Pharisee in the Temple in Luke 18:11 boasts that he is not like those who plunder others.
3. The word extends to one who extorts, who enriches themselves dishonestly, often by abusing their power or position. It is a crook, a scammer who respects no moral limits to gain.
4. In 1 Corinthians 5:10-11 and 6:10, Paul ranks the snatcher among the serious sinners from whom Christians must stay away, and who will not inherit the kingdom of God.
G0727.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb harpazō (to seize, to snatch). It primarily designates one who acts with this violence, hence the meaning of "one who snatches." The root always evokes the idea of a sudden and forced taking. In Genesis 49:27, the Greek version of the Old Testament uses a similar word to translate the idea of a wolf tearing its prey, which shows how biblical Greek understands this vocabulary of robbery.
G0727.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always with a very negative connotation. Jesus uses it once to paint false prophets: they outwardly resemble sheep but inwardly snatch and exploit (Matthew 7:15). Paul mentions it four times in 1 Corinthians, where he ranks the snatcher alongside the sexually immoral, the greedy, the idolater, and the drunkard: it is a serious sin, incompatible with life in Jesus Christ. The context shows that Paul is not speaking so much of the highway robber as of the greedy, of one who extorts, who takes advantage of their power to serve themselves.
G0727.portee: This word warns the Christian against two dangers. First, within oneself, not to become a snatcher: not to yield to greed, not to plunder others through cunning or violence. Secondly, to recognize false prophets and seducers who, under a beautiful appearance, seek only to exploit others. It is a call to vigilance and honesty in our relationships.

sens: Partial payment made in advance to guarantee a commitment
First part of a sum due, paid as a sign of seriousness
Pledge or security that ensures the fulfillment of a promise
Visible and tangible guarantee of a future promise
G0728.detail:
1. The earnest is primarily a payment made in advance when concluding a deal: it is a part of the total sum given immediately to prove that one is serious and will keep their word. In 2 Corinthians 1:22 and 5:5, Paul calls the Holy Spirit the "earnest" that God has placed in our hearts: like a first installment that guarantees that God will keep His promise to transform and completely save us.
2. The word also evokes the idea of a pledge or security: something concrete that is given in exchange for a promise. In Ephesians 1:14, the Spirit is called the "pledge" of our future inheritance, that is, the tangible sign that God has truly acquired us for Himself and that He will fulfill what He has promised.
3. More broadly, it is a visible guarantee of an invisible commitment: the word emphasizes that what we have now (the Spirit present in us) is the beginning and proof of what we will ultimately have (complete redemption, eternal inheritance). It is a bridge between the promise and its fulfillment.
G0728.origine: The Greek word ἀρραβών comes from the Hebrew עֲרָבוֹן (aroubôn), which means "pledge" or "security." The Phoenicians brought this term and this commercial practice to Greece, hence its presence in classical Greek. The Hebrew root evokes the idea of "mixing" or "exchanging": one gives something that remains in hand as proof of an agreement. The word has retained this concrete, commercial sense in the Bible.
G0728.emploi: Paul uses this word three times, always to speak of the Holy Spirit as God's guarantee. In 2 Corinthians 1:22, God has "sealed" and "put in our hearts the earnest of the Spirit": it is the sealing and the first installment of His commitment to us. In 2 Corinthians 5:5, God has "given us the earnest of the Spirit": it is the pledge that He will completely transform us. In Ephesians 1:14, the word becomes "pledge" and designates the Spirit as proof that we have been "acquired" by God and that final redemption will follow. Each time, the word transposes a commercial and material image to spiritual reality: the Spirit is what we have already received from God, and it is the promise of what we will receive.
G0728.portee: This word speaks directly to the heart of the Christian by reminding them that their faith is not vague: the Holy Spirit they receive at conversion is a real, tangible presence, the seal and guarantee that God will keep His promises. It is a call to trust: since we have already received this first installment, we can be certain of the redemption to come. The word encourages not to doubt: God does not abandon halfway those He has begun to transform.

sens: Having no seam where two pieces of fabric are joined
Entirely made from a single piece, woven as one
G0729.detail:
1. The word describes a garment that has no seams, meaning there is no line where thread has joined two edges of fabric. This is a particularly fine and labor-intensive weaving work: instead of sewing pieces together, the weaver creates the garment entirely in one weaving operation. John 19:23 shows us Jesus' tunic, "seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom" — a garment of great value and quality.
2. This absence of seams emphasizes the uniqueness and integrity of the garment: it forms an indivisible whole, without any break in its structure. This is why the soldiers who divide Jesus' garments notice this tunic and refuse to tear it apart, unlike the other pieces of clothing.
G0729.origine: The Greek word comes from the root ῥάπτω (rhaptô), which means "to sew." The privative prefix ἀ- (a-) means "without" or "not": thus ἄραφος (arraphos) literally means "without seams." It is the opposite of an ordinary garment where different pieces would be joined by sewing.
G0729.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 19:23, during the passion of Jesus. All four Gospels report the sharing of Jesus' garments among the Roman soldiers, but only John mentions the remarkable detail of this seamless tunic. This detail underscores the exceptional value and quality of this garment, as well as its integrity: it could not be divided like the other clothes. The soldiers recognize this special character and decide to keep it whole, which aligns with the Scripture referenced in the following verse.
G0729.portee: Jesus' seamless tunic symbolizes the unity and integrity of Christ. This detail, noted only by John, invites the reader to see beyond historical facts: even in the moment of stripping and ultimate humiliation, the integrity of the Lord remains. It can also speak to the Christian about preservation and completeness in Christ, who cannot be divided or fragmented.

sens: Person or animal of the male sex, as opposed to female
Firstborn male of a woman, subject to the law of consecration to the Lord
Adult man in social or relational contexts
Man in the affirmation of gender equality in Christ
G0730.detail:
1. The word designates the male sex in general, whether it refers to a human being or an animal. It is the primary contrast with the female: "God made man and woman" (Matthew 19:4, Mark 10:6). The image is that of the original biological distinction in creation.

2. In Mosaic law, the word applies to the firstborn male, who was to be consecrated to the Lord according to the law (Luke 2:23). This is a legal and religious application of the term: not only the sex, but a special position of the child.

3. In Romans 1:27, "man with man" refers to a relationship between two adult males in a context of carnal desire. Here the word takes on a moral hue, as it names an act that Paul condemns as contrary to the created nature.

4. In Galatians 3:28, "neither male nor female" states the abolition in the Church of the sexual distinction as a principle of value or access to grace: in Christ, biological sex has no salvific significance; all are equal.
G0730.origine: The Greek word ἄρσην (arsèn) or ἄρρην (arrèn) is an ancient Greek adjective found in the Attic dialect. It comes from an Indo-European root denoting manliness and strength. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it regularly translates the Hebrew זָכָר (zakār), which literally means "the one who remembers" or "the male," a common term for the male sex in the laws of Israel. The family of the Greek word includes derivatives related to strength and masculinity.
G0730.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament according to the Segond. Matthew and Mark use it in the singular to cite the creation of man and woman (Matthew 19:4, Mark 10:6), referencing Genesis 1:27. Luke uses it for the firstborn male subject to the law of consecration (Luke 2:23). In Romans 1:27, Paul uses it twice: first to designate men abandoning natural use, then to name sexual relations between males, a neutral term that places moral emphasis on the act, not on the person. Galatians 3:28 uses it abstractly and equally: "neither male nor female" expresses the abolition of distinction as a Christian criterion. Revelation 12 uses it for the male child of the woman (12:5, 13), a prophetic figure of the Messiah.
G0730.portee: This word refers to a created reality: the male sex in its biological and social essence. For the believer, it reminds us that man and woman are created together in the image of God, and that this difference is good. At the same time, Galatians 3:28 frees the Christian from hierarchy: in Christ, sex is no longer a barrier to grace or a criterion of spiritual identity. Romans 1:27 highlights how the Gospel evaluates human acts against the backdrop of the created order and calls for repentance.

sens: That cannot be expressed in words
That exceeds the capacity of human language
That is beyond what can be said or communicated
G0731.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what cannot simply be said or stated — something that remains unspoken, that has not yet been put into words. This is the most basic idea: we do not speak of this thing; it remains silent.

2. But it also means what *cannot* be said, because it exceeds language itself. Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians 12:4 for the mysterious words he heard in heaven: they are so extraordinary, so far from ordinary experience, that no human tongue could express or convey them faithfully. Heaven and its wonders surpass human speech.
G0731.origine: The word comes from the Greek negative prefix "a-" ("not") and "rhêtos," which means "spoken" or "expressible" — the latter coming from the root "rhéô" ("to flow," "to stream"). By this imagery, what flows is speech: what can be expressed "flows" from the mouth. The ineffable is what cannot flow into words. The word is rare in ancient Greek and in the New Testament.
G0731.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 12:4, where Paul recounts a mystical experience in the third heaven. He heard "ineffable" words — secrets, heavenly revelations so deep and extraordinary that he is forbidden to express them to other men. The usage shows that the word serves to express ineffability: not only should something not be said (in obedience), but it cannot be said (due to the limits of language). It is a point of apophaticism — recognizing that there are divine realities that no earthly words can grasp.
G0731.portee: This word reminds the believer that the experience of God transcends words. When we pray, when we encounter the Lord, words often fail — and that is normal. Paul shows this: even an apostle, seized by God, must remain silent about certain mysteries. This invites humility in our language about the things of God and encourages seeking, beyond words, silent communion with Him.

sens: One who suffers from a physical illness
One who is weak or infirm
Figuratively, one who is spiritually or morally deficient
G0732.detail:
1. A sick person is someone whose body is affected by an illness or infirmity. When Jesus stepped out of the boat, "he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion for them, and he healed the sick" (Matthew 14:14). The term refers to those who suffer physically and need healing. In Mark 6:13, the apostles "anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them," showing that illness is a visible and treatable condition.
2. The word can also express a general weakness or frailty. In 1 Corinthians 11:30, Paul writes: "That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died," suggesting a condition of weakness that exposes one to divine judgment.
3. Spiritually, being sick can denote a moral or spiritual failing. Mark 16:18 promises believers that "they will lay hands on the sick, and the sick will recover" — an image of the restoration that faith in Christ brings, which goes beyond mere physical healing.
G0732.origine: The Greek word arrōstos comes from the root rhōnnumi (to strengthen, to fortify), preceded by the negative prefix a-: it refers to one who is not strengthened, weakened. The basic image is that of a missing strength, a weakness of the body. In Hebrew and Aramaic, this word often corresponds to chala (sickness), which also expresses the idea of bodily weakness.
G0732.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always to refer to the sick who receive healing. Three occurrences are in Mark (6:5, 6:13, 16:18), one in Matthew (14:14), and one in 1 Corinthians (11:30). Mark regularly emphasizes the apostles' actions toward the sick: Jesus lays hands on them (6:5), the disciples anoint them with oil and heal them (6:13). In Matthew, it is Jesus' compassion for the sick that is highlighted. Paul, in 1 Corinthians 11:30, uses the term to explain a consequence of divine judgment: physical ailments and death strike those who profane the Lord's Supper. The context is always that of healing or, in Paul's case, human frailty in the face of judgment.
G0732.portee: This word reminds us that illnesses are a reality that Jesus sees and is moved by. The healing of the sick is a central sign of the coming of the Kingdom of God: it shows that Jesus does not remain indifferent to suffering but acts with power and compassion. For the Christian, the fact that the apostles heal the sick indicates that the Gospel includes a dimension of concrete relief from physical distress, linked to the total restoration that God promises.

sens: one who commits acts against nature with someone of the same sex
a person whose conduct is abominable and shameful
G0733.detail:
1. The word specifically refers to one who engages in sexual relations with a person of the same sex, particularly a man with a man. This conduct is severely condemned in the Old Testament and by the law of Moses, and Paul classifies it among the serious sins that exclude one from the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:9).
2. More broadly, it characterizes a person whose behavior is deeply shameful and contrary to righteousness. This is why Paul associates it in 1 Timothy 1:10 with kidnappers, liars, and perjurers: all behaviors that oppose "sound doctrine," that is, the healthy teaching of Christ.
G0733.origine: The Greek word is composed of two terms: "ἄρσην" (arsēn = male, man) and "κοιτή" (koitē = bed, marital relation). Together, they literally form "one who lies with males." This word was created by the Greek translators of the Old Testament or by Christian authors to express a reality that the Mosaic law clearly condemns, particularly in Leviticus. It is a directly composed word, constructed to precisely name this act.
G0733.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two cited passages. In 1 Corinthians 6:9, Paul lists the categories of people who will not inherit the kingdom of God: among them are idolaters, adulterers, thieves, and "the infamous." In 1 Timothy 1:10, Paul includes this word in a broader list of those who act "against sound doctrine" — including kidnappers, liars, and perjurers. In both cases, it serves to classify a serious sin, a transgression of God's moral law.
G0733.portee: This word reminds Christians that the Bible establishes a moral standard for human sexuality, inscribed in creation and confirmed by the law. It calls for repentance and transformation in Christ, for Paul adds after listing the sins in 1 Corinthians 6:9-11: "And such were some of you; but you were washed, you were sanctified..." — showing that forgiveness and renewal are possible for those who turn to Jesus.

sens: apostolic companion of Paul
G0734.detail: Artemas is a first-century Christian mentioned by Paul in his letter to Titus. Paul plans to send him to Titus in Crete to replace him in his ministry, which shows that Artemas was a reliable collaborator capable of leading a church. His name means "gift of Artemis" or "healthy and vigorous."
G0734.origine: The name Artemas is of Greek origin, formed from elements originally designating a gift or blessing from the goddess Artemis. It is a name bearing religious significance in Greco-Roman culture, although for Paul and the early church it simply denotes a brother in Christ.
G0734.emploi: Artemas appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 3:12. Paul, writing to Titus who oversees the church in Crete, informs him that he will send either Artemas or Tychicus to relieve him of his duties and allow him to join Paul in Nicopolis where Paul plans to spend the winter. This mention shows that Artemas was regarded as a capable and trustworthy worker within the Pauline apostolic network.
G0734.portee: The mention of Artemas reminds the reader that the apostolic mission relied on a network of faithful collaborators, often little visible in history but essential to the development of the early church. His name speaks to us of concrete brotherhood and interdependence among the pioneers of Christianity.

sens: Pagan goddess of the Greco-Roman world, particularly venerated in Asia Minor
Object of urban and commercial worship whose economic prestige mobilized an entire city
G0735.detail:
1. Diana is the goddess that the Ephesians worshiped, particularly in the Asian context where she had a very important sanctuary. She is a female deity of the Greek and Roman world, but she was linked to the culture of Asia Minor and enjoyed intense popular veneration (Acts 19:27-28).
2. The worship of Diana was not only a matter of religious piety but also a major source of economic revenue for the city: silversmiths like Demetrius made their living by crafting small temples and objects of worship dedicated to the goddess (Acts 19:24). When the Gospel threatens this commerce, the entire city revolts (Acts 19:34-35).
G0735.origine: The Greek name Ἄρτεμις refers to the Greek goddess Artemis, whom the Latins called Diana (hence the translation Diana). In Asia, this worship took on a particular form and dominated the life of Ephesus, where the temple of Artemis was one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. Although she is a deity of the Greco-Roman pantheon, the biblical narrative focuses on her Asian incarnation and her religious and commercial influence.
G0735.emploi: Diana appears five times in the New Testament, exclusively in the account of the riot in Ephesus in chapter 19 of Acts. Paul converted enough people to shake the commerce of religious objects related to this worship. The merchants and the townspeople are in an uproar: they shout, "Great is Diana of the Ephesians!" (Acts 19:28, 34), thus affirming their civic and religious pride. The magistrate even acknowledges that Ephesus is famous for being the guardian of her temple and her statue, reputed to have fallen from heaven (Acts 19:35). This passage illustrates how a deeply rooted popular cult in a city can stand as a bulwark against the Gospel when its material interests are threatened.
G0735.portee: This mention of Diana reveals how the Gospel of Jesus comes into conflict not only with idols but with the economy and urban pride that are attached to them. It also shows that the riot arises less from sincere religious conviction than from the fear of losing a livelihood. For the Christian today, it is a reminder that true conversion changes priorities: it no longer seeks to enrich itself through religion but to serve Jesus alone.

sens: Forward or upper sail of a ship
By extension, maneuvering sail used to steer the boat
G0736.detail:
1. The mizzen sail is a sail located at the front or at the top of the mast of an ancient ship. It gets its name from the verb that means "to attach" or "to secure": it is a sail that is firmly secured to the mast so that it can withstand the wind. In Acts 27:40, during the shipwreck of Paul's boat, the sailors "loosen the ropes of the rudders" and "set the mizzen sail to the wind" in an attempt to steer the ship toward the shore: this sail is a maneuvering tool, essential for controlling the direction of the boat in a crisis situation.
2. Figuratively, this sail represents the instrument that allows one to govern the ship: it symbolizes mastery, the direction taken in a difficult situation. The sailors know that by setting this particular sail to the wind, they can steer their course toward salvation.
G0736.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb that means "to attach" or "to secure firmly." The mizzen sail is thus named because it must be securely fastened to the mast to withstand the forces of the wind. It is a technical maritime term, specific to ancient navigation, and it appears only once in the New Testament: in Acts 27:40, in the dramatic account of the shipwreck.
G0736.emploi: This word appears only once in the entire Bible: in Acts 27:40, at the heart of the account of Paul's shipwreck. The context is that of a catastrophic storm in the Mediterranean. The sailors of the ship, having lost all hope of saving themselves with the main sails, decide to use the mizzen sail as a last resort to steer the boat toward the shore. This unique mention shows that Luke, the author of Acts, is well acquainted with the technical realities of the maritime world of his time and reports the details accurately: the mizzen sail is the ultimate maneuvering instrument when other means of navigation have failed.
G0736.portee: For the Christian reader, this mention of the mizzen sail in the account of the shipwreck illustrates how, even in the midst of the greatest storms, God places in the hands of men the means to persevere and seek salvation. The sailors do not give up; they use every available resource. This detail reminds us that faith does not exclude prudent action and human ingenuity in the face of crises.

sens: The present moment, the current instant, as opposed to the past or the future
What is happening or occurring at this precise moment
The current state, the present situation
The immediate consequence of an action, what has just been done
At the moment when the word is spoken, in the immediacy of the discourse
G0737.detail:
1. The word denotes the current moment, the one in which the people of the text speak or act. Jesus says to Nicodemus: "You do not understand now, but you will understand later" (John 13:7), distinguishing the present from the moment when understanding will come. It is the instant that opposes the past or the future.
2. It emphasizes the accuracy, the precision of the moment: "Do you think that I cannot call on my Father, who would at once give me more than twelve legions of angels?" (Matthew 26:53). The word insists on the immediate possibility, here and right now.
3. It describes the current condition of someone or something: "How then does he see now?" ask the neighbors of the blind man (John 9:19). The word captures a change of state, what is true at that moment.
4. It marks the direct succession: "until now" means "up to this moment, continuously from the past." Paul writes: "being slandered, we speak kindly; we have become like the scum of the world, until now" (1 Corinthians 4:13).
5. Used in dialogue, it emphasizes the immediacy of the word: "Why can't I follow you now?" asks Peter (John 13:37), giving his question a present urgency and force.
G0737.origine: The Greek word ἄρτι comes from an Indo-European root related to adjustment, to closeness. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it mostly translates עַתָּה (attâ), which literally means "the moment that comes." It is a temporal adverb that focuses on presence, on what is immediately there. Greek has only one word for "now," unlike French, which can say "à présent" or "en ce moment": ἄρτι is the natural and brief way to designate the strict present.
G0737.emploi: The word appears 36 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospel of John and in the Pauline letters. It is very common in dialogues: Jesus uses it to mark the limit between what the disciples do not yet understand and what they will understand. Jesus' opponents use it to contest the present ("How does he see now?" John 9:19). Paul uses it to speak of his current state ("until now we have suffered hunger," 1 Corinthians 4:13) or to state immediately valid truths ("For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face. Now I know in part," 1 Corinthians 13:12). The word creates a tension: it shows that something has changed (the miracle, the revelation) or that something is in the process of changing (the time of the last days has now begun, Revelation 12:10).
G0737.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that faith is not a distant or abstract matter: it concerns the moment when one reads, when one believes, when one acts. When Jesus says "now" in the Gospel, he invites to a present decision. When Paul writes "now" in speaking of suffering or imperfect knowledge, he anchors the Christian experience in the reality of the day. It is a word that pulls the reader from dreaming to life as it is.

sens: child who has just been born, from one day to a few months
figuratively, young Christian who is just beginning their spiritual life
G0738.detail:
