1. The word literally designates a child who has just been born, freshly out of the mother's womb. It conveys the idea of freshness and extreme novelty.
2. Peter uses it figuratively to speak of young Christians or those who have just converted and received the Holy Spirit. Just as a newborn infant needs pure milk to grow, the young believer needs the Word of God, simple and pure, to develop spiritually (1 Peter 2:2).
G0738.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: « arti » (meaning « just, at this moment ») and « gennétos » (« begotten, born », from the root « gennao » which means « to give birth »). It is a compound that paints the idea of an extremely recent, almost immediate birth. The word is rare in the New Testament and appears mainly in the medical and descriptive literature of the ancient world.
G0738.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 2:2. Peter uses it to urge young converts to desire the Word of God as a newborn desires mother's milk. This comparison is striking: just as a newborn child has a natural and urgent appetite for the milk that nourishes and helps them grow, the believer who has just been spiritually born must hunger for the pure Gospel to progress toward spiritual maturity and salvation.
G0738.portee: This image of the newborn reminds us that entering the Christian faith is a true birth, a radical beginning. It also teaches us that our spiritual growth depends on simple and pure nourishment: the Word of God. For the young Christian, this word calls for humility and spiritual hunger; for those who are growing in Christ, it reminds us that we all started as newborns in faith, and that the main food for our growth remains the Word.

sens: That is complete, without lack, prepared for its function
That is fit, capable, competent for a task
That possesses everything necessary to act well
G0739.detail:
1. The word describes something complete, lacking nothing — a whole where all the pieces are present and well-fitted. In 2 Timothy 3:17, the man of God is described as « complete » through the Scriptures: he now possesses everything he needs spiritually.
2. A complete man is fit, capable, competent to undertake a work — he has the required skills. This is precisely what Paul affirms: the man of God who has received training from the Scriptures becomes competent and capable of every good work.
3. Being complete means being equipped, supplied with everything suitable. It conveys the idea of complete preparation, where nothing has been forgotten or left aside.
G0739.origine: The Greek word ἄρτιος comes from a root that evokes the idea of « adapting » or « fitting » — like pieces that fit perfectly together. It is infrequent in the New Testament and reflects the biblical image of a life shaped, completed, and made functional by the Word of God.
G0739.emploi: ἄρτιος appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:17. Paul uses it to describe the man of God — one who feeds on and learns from the Holy Scriptures — as having become complete and fit for every good work. This is the fruit of biblical training: the Scriptures make the man of God « complete ». The context is one of faithfulness to the Scriptures as the ultimate source of spiritual training and moral competence.
G0739.portee: This word invites the Christian to see the Holy Scriptures not as a fragmented collection, but as the complete instrument of their spiritual training. It makes them « complete » — prepared, capable, confident — for every work that God sets before them. It is a word of encouragement: by feeding on the Word, one does not remain unfinished, lacking nothing to serve well.

sens: food made of flour and water baked in an oven
piece or quantity of bread
action of eating, meal
food in general, sustenance
the showbread in the temple
Christ himself, bread of life
G0740.detail:
1. Bread is the basic food: flour and water transformed by baking. It is the product that people make and eat daily. Jesus speaks of it in temptation: « If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become bread » (Matthew 4:3).

2. The word also designates an individual loaf, a quantity that can be counted and distributed. During the multiplication, Jesus takes five loaves and multiplies them to feed five thousand men (Matthew 14:17, Luke 9:13).

3. « Taking meals » literally means « eating bread ». The Pharisees reproach Jesus' disciples for taking their meals « with unclean hands » (Mark 7:5): it is the time of the meal, the sharing of bread.

4. Broadly, bread represents the food needed to live. This is why Jesus teaches to pray « Give us this day our daily bread » (Matthew 6:11): it is asking for what is necessary to subsist.

5. In the temple, the showbread (also called the bread of the Presence) was consecrated bread placed on the table of the sanctuary as an offering to God (Matthew 12:4).

6. In a spiritual sense, Jesus says « I am the bread of life » (John 6:35): he compares himself to bread, this essential food, to show that he himself is what we need for eternal life.
G0740.origine: The Greek word « artos » comes from an ancient root meaning the action of preparing, arranging, ordering. It translates the Hebrew « lèkem », bread. Bread being the fundamental food of every Mediterranean and Middle Eastern civilization, this word was naturally very common. Its root evokes the idea of what is prepared, shaped, resulting from a work of arrangement: bread is indeed the fruit of the work of preparation and baking.
G0740.emploi: The word « bread » is used 91 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. It appears in very varied contexts: the temptations of Jesus in the desert (Matthew 4), daily meals, the Last Supper where Jesus breaks the bread and gives it to his disciples (Matthew 26:26, Luke 22:19), passages where Jesus multiplies the loaves to feed the crowds (Matthew 14:17-19), and especially Jesus' discourses in John 6 where he presents himself as the living bread that came down from heaven. In Acts, bread accompanies the fellowship of the early Christians « in the breaking of bread » (Acts 2:42, 2:46). The word naturally shifts from the material sense (the food) to the figurative sense (spiritual nourishment, Christ himself) depending on the context.
G0740.portee: Bread reminds us that God provides for our daily material needs: we must trust him for food, as Jesus teaches in the Lord's Prayer. But more profoundly, when Jesus declares himself « bread of life », he invites the believer to receive him as their spiritual food, the one who alone can satisfy the deep longing of the human heart. At every shared meal, at every breaking of bread in the Christian community, we remember that Jesus gave his life and that we depend on him to truly live.

sens: To add flavor to food by adding salt or spices
To make something immaterial pleasant, attractive, or flavorful
G0741.detail:
1. To season literally means to add salt or other seasonings to food to enhance its flavor. This is the concrete image of the verb: "Salt is good; but if the salt has lost its flavor, with what will it be seasoned?" (Luke 14:34). Without salt, food is bland and unappetizing.
2. Figuratively, to season applies to speech: "Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt" (Colossians 4:6). Here, "salt" represents what makes speech pleasant, useful, and memorable — words that are neither bland nor boring, but alive and full of wisdom.
G0741.origine: The verb comes from the Greek root *art-*, which evokes arrangement and order. In classical ancient Greek, it primarily denotes the action of arranging or preparing. The culinary use (to season) is well attested in Greek comic authors. The association with salt, a biblical symbol of preservation and flavor, enriches the meaning: salt "seasons" and preserves.
G0741.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, all in contexts related to salt. Two occurrences are found in Jesus' saying about salt (Mark 9:50 and Luke 14:34) — they repeat the same saying in two different gospels, with the same concrete image: tasteless salt cannot season anyone. The third occurrence in Paul (Colossians 4:6) transposes the image to the moral and spiritual realm: conversation must be "seasoned with salt," meaning filled with grace and discernment. This passage shows how the word shifts from the concrete to the figurative.
G0741.portee: This word invites the Christian not to let their speech be bland and insignificant. Jesus teaches that salt has a function — to give flavor and preserve — and that the believer must likewise have a visible impact in the world. For Paul, the salt of speech is grace mixed with wisdom, which makes the testimony attractive and relevant. The Christian life is not meant to be gray or boring, but flavorful and edifying.

sens: Ancestor of Christ mentioned in the genealogy of Luke
G0742.detail: Arphaxad is a biblical figure mentioned only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:36, in the long genealogy tracing back from Jesus to Adam. He is presented as the son of Cainan and the father of Shem (although Cainan is a specific addition to Luke's genealogy, and other biblical genealogies differ slightly on this point). This name appears in the chain of ancestors that establishes Jesus' connection with primordial humanity and with Noah, the survivor of the Flood.
G0742.origine: The name Arphaxad comes from the Hebrew אַרְפַּכְשַׁד (Arphakshad). Its exact etymology is debated, but it may evoke in Hebrew a region or a notion of "fortress" or "domain." This name also appears in the Old Testament (Genesis 10:22 and 11:10), where he is presented as the son of Shem and ancestor of the messianic line. Biblical tradition places him among the descendants of Shem, symbolizing the promised line that will lead to Abraham and ultimately to Jesus.
G0742.emploi: Arphaxad appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:36, at the heart of the genealogy of Jesus traced by Luke. This genealogy follows a reverse direction from that of Genesis, tracing back from Jesus to Adam and passing through all the important ancestors. Arphaxad occupies his place in the regular succession of generations, as a link in the continuous chain connecting Christ to ancient humanity. Luke includes this figure to affirm that Jesus descends from the eternal lineage and promise of God from the very beginning.
G0742.portee: This mention reminds the reader that Jesus is part of the human history from the very start — not a mysterious newcomer, but the culmination of a genealogy traced continuously back to Adam. It emphasizes that salvation is not a divine improvisation, but the fulfillment of a promise that spans all ages and generations of humanity.

sens: Angel of the highest rank in the celestial hierarchy
Divine messenger invested with particular authority
G0743.detail:
1. The archangel is an angel who occupies a prominent position among celestial beings — not just a messenger, but a chief, a prince of the angelic army. In 1 Thessalonians 4:16, it is at the voice of an archangel that the Lord will descend from heaven to resurrect the dead in Christ: the context suggests a major figure of the invisible world, capable of delivering a divine command that shakes the entire universe.
2. Michael, the archangel named in Jude 1:9, contends for the body of Moses against the devil himself and refuses to pronounce against him a railing judgment: this passage shows that the archangel possesses an authority and dignity that place him directly in confrontation with the powers of evil, as a representative of divine authority.
G0743.origine: The word "archangel" results from the composition of two Greek words: "archi-" (chief, first) and "angelos" (angel, messenger). It literally designates the "chief of angels" or the "leading angel." This notion of angelic hierarchy, with higher-ranking angels governing the others, reflects a view of the invisible world that is very present in New Testament theology and partly inherited from ancient Jewish thought.
G0743.emploi: The word "archangel" appears only twice in the New Testament. In 1 Thessalonians 4:16, written by Paul to the Christians in Thessalonica, an archangel (unnamed) plays a central role in the supreme eschatological event: the Parousia, the return of the Lord. In Jude 1:9, the archangel Michael is explicitly designated as the figure who confronts the devil during the dispute for the body of Moses. These two occurrences underscore the exceptional importance of archangels in the divine economy: they are not ordinary angels, but major actors in final realities and spiritual battles.
G0743.portee: The doctrine of archangels reminds the believer that the spiritual world has a structure and hierarchy, and that God has powerful and worthy celestial servants to accomplish His purposes. The mention of the archangel at the resurrection of the dead emphasizes that our hope is rooted in a cosmic order of which God alone is the master. Michael's battle against the devil for the body of Moses invites the Christian to recognize that spiritual struggles are real and that God actively participates in them through His messengers.

sens: which dates back to the origins, to the beginning
which is from a long time ago, from the past
which belongs to the old, bygone order
G0744.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what goes back to the origin, the starting point: when Jesus says, "You have heard that it was said to the ancients" (Matthew 5:21), he is referring to the commandments given from the beginning to Israel, which were established "long ago" (Acts 15:7).
2. It then describes what belongs to the past, to a bygone era: the disciples imagine that Jesus could be "one of the ancient prophets" resurrected (Luke 9:8, 9:19), that is, a prophet from days gone by.
3. Finally, the word characterizes the old order destined to disappear: Paul writes, "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation: old things have passed away" (2 Corinthians 5:17), for Christ inaugurates a new order.
G0744.origine: The word comes from the root "archè" (beginning, origin): an "ancient" is literally what goes back to the origins. It stands in opposition to what is new or recent. In the Septuagint (the Greek version of the Old Testament), it translates the Hebrew word "qedem" which also means "ancient" and "before" (that which comes first). This family of words expresses the idea that an ancient thing is one that began first, which is original.
G0744.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and the Epistles. Matthew uses it twice to refer to the commandments of the Old Covenant (5:21, 5:33): it is what was established from the beginning for Israel. Luke uses it to speak of the ancient prophets (9:8, 9:19), figures of what belongs to the distant past. Paul imbues it with theological meaning by opposing it to the "new" (2 Corinthians 5:17): the old is the expired regime, while the new is the order inaugurated by Christ. Revelation applies it to the Devil (12:9, 20:2), presenting him as an ancient being, original in his malice.
G0744.portee: This word invites the Christian to discern between the old order and the new order brought by Christ. It shows that the Law has not disappeared — it has its "ancient" authority, of divine origin — but that it is surpassed by a higher reality. For the believer, the word reminds that life in Christ is not a reformation of the past, but a break with a bygone regime: "Old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new."

sens: Son of Herod the Great, king of Judea, Samaria, and Idumea
G0745.detail: Archelaus is one of the sons of Herod the Great who received a portion of his father's kingdom after his death. He ruled over Judea, Samaria, and Idumea, the most important territories of the Herodian kingdom. It was upon learning that Archelaus had become king that Joseph decided not to return to Judea with the child Jesus, but to head toward Galilee, fearing Archelaus's reputation (Matthew 2:22).
G0745.origine: The Greek name Archelaus literally means "he who governs the people" (archè = command, laos = people). It is a dynastic name borne by several Hellenistic kings before him.
G0745.emploi: Archelaus appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew's account concerning the return of the Holy Family from Egypt. This historical event takes place after the death of Herod the Great (4 BC), when the kingdom was divided among his heirs. Archelaus received the richest but also the most troubled territories, and his reputation as a tyrant justified Joseph's fears.
G0745.portee: This mention of Archelaus reminds us that Jesus was born in a concrete and sometimes perilous political context. It shows how God directs historical events and guides his servants through difficult circumstances, appearing to Joseph in a dream to protect him from this tyrannical prince.

sens: The starting point, the moment when something begins
What comes first in a series, the origin of an action or a word
The edge or corner of a material thing
Authority, dominion, the power to command
In God and Christ, eternity, the source and principle of all
G0746.detail:
1. The beginning is the moment when an action or process starts. It is the starting point, the "before" of a story. When the Bible says "from the beginning" (1 John 2:24), it refers to the moment when the message was first heard, at the start of the path of faith.

2. It is also what comes first in a succession: the beginning of a series of signs, like the birth pains that come at the "beginning" (Matthew 24:8), or the first miracle of Jesus at Cana (John 2:11).

3. Concretely, this word also designates the corners or edges of a thing, like the four corners of a tablecloth that Peter sees in a vision (Acts 10:11).

4. The word also means authority and power: a magistrate who exercises "dominion" over a city (Luke 12:11) or the "principalities" that Paul enumerates among the spiritual powers (Ephesians 6:12).

5. For God and Christ, "beginning" expresses eternity and the absolute source: God is the Beginning (Revelation 21:6), and Christ, as the active principle of creation, is "the beginning" who creates and sustains all things (Colossians 1:18; Revelation 3:14).
G0746.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that evokes the idea of "beginning" or "leading." That is why it means both the start (that by which one begins) and authority (the one who begins, who leads). In ancient Greek, it often translates the Hebrew "reš" (head, chief, first) and "qédem" (ancientness, from before). This dual dimension—beginning and command—reflects the same reality: the one who is first is also the one who leads.
G0746.emploi: The word "beginning" appears 55 times in the New Testament, particularly in the Gospels of John and in the epistles. It is first used in a temporal sense: the beginning of a story, teaching, or action (John 16:4, Luke 1:2, 1 John 2:24). It also designates the moment when a series of calamities begins: the "beginning of sorrows" that precede the end of times (Matthew 24:8). The word takes on a political or social meaning when it speaks of magistrates and authorities exercising power (Luke 12:11). On a spiritual level, Paul uses it to describe the "principalities" and "powers" that govern the world (Ephesians 6:12; Colossians 1:16). Finally, applied to God and Christ, the word becomes almost mystical: it expresses their eternal character and their role as the creative source of all that exists (John 1:1; Revelation 21:6; Colossians 1:18).
G0746.portee: This word reminds us that everything has a beginning—except God and Christ. They are the Eternal, the one who was "in the beginning" before any creation (John 1:1). For the Christian, this means that our faith has a concrete starting point, a moment when we heard and received the Gospel, and that we must "hold fast" (Hebrews 3:14). It is also an invitation to see that Christ is not just a power among others: he is the Beginning, the one who creates and governs all things, visible and invisible.

sens: The one who begins or inaugurates something, who is its founder or initiator
The one who leads, who guides a group of people toward a destination or goal
Chief or leader endowed with sovereign authority
G0747.detail: 1. The word primarily designates the one who inaugurates or begins something — who lays the foundation or is its author. This conveys the idea of beginning, of initiative: in Hebrews 12:2, Jesus is called the "author and finisher of faith," meaning he inaugurated it and brought it to completion. 2. The meaning nuances into "the one who leads" or "who guides": in Hebrews 2:10, Jesus is the "Prince of their salvation," the one who guides them to glory by himself passing through sufferings. He is a guide who walks ahead of his disciples. 3. Finally, the word means "prince" or "sovereign," that is, a chief endowed with royal or princely authority: in Acts 3:15 and 5:31, Jesus is presented as the "Prince" whom God raised to His right hand, a figure of authority and divine power.
G0747.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and combines the idea of "beginning" (archē) with that of "leading" or "bringing." It etymologically designates the one who is at the origin, who begins or initiates. This Greek word translates in the Hebrew of the Old Testament terms like "head" (rosh) or "chief" (nasi), showing that it is a figure of authority and primacy. The image is that of a guide who walks at the forefront, of a founder who takes the first steps on a path that others will follow.
G0747.emploi: The word appears 4 times only in the New Testament, all usages concerning Jesus Christ. In Acts (3:15 and 5:31), Peter uses this title to present the risen Jesus as a figure of power and authority raised by God. In Hebrews, the word takes on a more theological nuance: in 2:10, Jesus is the "Prince of salvation" who leads His children to glory; in 12:2, he is the founder and perfecter of faith. Each usage emphasizes the directing and authoritative aspect of Jesus: he initiates salvation, guides to glory, and accomplishes what he begins.
G0747.portee: This word reveals that Jesus is not simply an example or a teacher among others: he is the one who opens the way of salvation, who walks at the head of His children. For the believer, this is assurance: the Christ who calls us to follow is not an uncertain guide, but the Prince endowed with divine authority. He initiated our salvation and will be its finisher — he will bring it to completion.

sens: Pertaining to or relating to the high priest and his function
Concerning the dignity, authority, or worship of the high priest
G0748.detail:
1. The word describes everything concerning the Jewish high priest: his charge, his role in worship, his religious authority. In Acts 4:6, it qualifies the "chief priests," that is, the members of the family or class of high priests who collectively exercised major influence in the Sanhedrin.
2. Figuratively, it applies to what pertains to the dignity and sovereign power attached to this supreme religious function — decisions, acts, responsibilities that emanate from this high priestly position.
G0748.origine: The word is formed from the Greek "archierús" (high priest, literally "first priest"), composed of "arkhē" (beginning, first place, power) and "hierús" (priest). It is an adjective that connects everything being discussed to this eminent function. The background is Jewish: the high priest was the chief of worship at the temple and the highest religious magistrate of the nation of Israel.
G0748.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 4:6. It designates the group of "chief priests" — probably the living former high priests and their family members who held influence. These men are part of the Sanhedrin who interrogate Peter and John after the healing of the lame man at the Beautiful Gate. The use of the word emphasizes their status as a religious elite endowed with particular power in contemporary Jewish life.
G0748.portee: This word reminds the reader of the major opposition that the early Christians faced: that of the Jewish religious authorities. The high priest and his entourage, far from recognizing Jesus as Messiah, persecuted those who preached in his name. This sheds light on the gravity of the tensions between the nascent Church and the Jewish religious establishment of the first century.

sens: The supreme leader of worship in the temple of Jerusalem, who presided over the priesthood of Israel
In the Gospels, the one who led the accusations against Jesus during his trial
In the plural, the former chief priests, the former priests, and the families of high priests who collectively formed the Jewish religious elite
G0749.detail:
1. The high priest was the chief responsible for all sacrifices and worship at the temple of Jerusalem: it was the highest rank of the Jewish priesthood. Mark 14:63 shows him tearing his garments during Jesus' trial, which was his solemn gesture of protest.
2. In the New Testament, the serving high priest plays a central role in the condemnation of Jesus: he presides over the Sanhedrin tribunal and interrogates Jesus about his identity (Mark 14:60-61). John 18:24 shows how he remains active throughout the trial before Pilate.
3. Very often, the Gospels use the plural "chief priests" to refer to both the serving high priest and all other living former high priests, as well as the leaders of the main priestly families: they formed the supreme religious authority in Jerusalem (Matthew 2:4, Luke 23:10). These men collectively opposed Jesus.
G0749.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: "archè" (principle, supreme power) and "hiéreus" (priest). It literally means "the priest who has supreme power." In Hebrew, the term corresponds to "kohen hagadol" (the high priest) or "rosh hakohanim" (the chief of priests). The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) used this same word to designate the Hebrew high priest, establishing a direct link with the cultic tradition of Israel.
G0749.emploi: This word appears 120 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Gospels and Acts. In the singular, it designates the high priest of Jerusalem in office at each time: in Luke 3:2, Annas and Caiaphas are both mentioned as high priests (or rather, one in office, the other formerly). In the plural, the word constantly returns to describe the block of religious power that opposes Jesus: Matthew 27:12 and 27:20 show how the "chief priests" incite the crowd to demand Jesus' death. After Pentecost, they also oppose the apostles (Acts 23:5, where Paul admits to having shown disrespect to the high priest). The word reflects the organized and institutional hostility of the Jewish religious system toward Jesus and the early Church.
G0749.portee: For the Christian reader, the central role of the high priest and his peers in the condemnation of Jesus shows how established religious power opposed the Messiah: it is a call to examine which authority we truly listen to. But the New Testament also reveals that Jesus himself is the perfect "high priest" (Hebrews 2:17, 3:1), who does not depend on any human succession and whose unique sacrifice replaces all the former temple rituals. This truth frees the believer from dependence on an intermediary religious authority.

sens: Chief shepherd who governs other shepherds
The one who guides the flock with the highest authority
Figure of the risen Christ who watches over all believers
G0750.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a chief shepherd, one who commands other shepherds and the entire flock — someone who has sovereign authority over all the shepherds and their sheep. It is a title of power and responsibility.

2. The image is that of a supreme shepherd, not just a simple flock keeper, but one who reigns over the entire people of God. Peter applies it to Christ in 1 Peter 5:4, where he calls Jesus the "chief shepherd" who reigns above all the shepherds of the Church.

3. For believers, it is a promise: when this supreme shepherd appears, all those who have kept the faith will receive a crown of glory that will never fade away. The title reveals that Christ is not just a guide among others, but the unique Lord of the flock.
G0750.origine: The word combines "archi" (which means chief, first) and "poimèn" (shepherd). This formation follows the same logic as "archon" (chief) or "archangel" (supreme angel). In Greek, it was used to designate the chiefs of tribes and high officials. It is a term of prestige and command.
G0750.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 5:4. Peter addresses the elders (shepherds) of the churches and reminds them that there is a supreme shepherd above them: Jesus Christ. This context shows that the title exalts Christ's unique authority over all those who serve Him. It contrasts with human shepherds: they are temporary and visible, He is eternal and sovereign.
G0750.portee: This title strengthens Christians in crisis or doubt: you have a supreme Chief who watches over you, not just human leaders. For shepherds, it is a humbling yet comforting reminder that they are accountable to Jesus Himself, and that their authority is merely delegated. For all believers, it is the assurance that the risen Christ actively governs His Church.

sens: Christian from the city of Colossae, companion of Paul
G0751.detail: Archippus is a Christian disciple mentioned twice in the New Testament, both in letters from Paul written around 60 AD. He lives in Colossae, in Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey). In the letter to Philemon, Paul refers to him as a "fellow soldier" (Philemon 1:2), indicating that he is actively participating in the missionary work alongside Paul. In his letter to the Colossians, Paul personally exhorts him: "Say to Archippus: Take heed to the ministry which you have received in the Lord, that you may fulfill it" (Colossians 4:17). This exhortation suggests that Archippus has received a specific responsibility in the local Church and that Paul wants to ensure he fulfills it faithfully.
G0751.origine: The name Ἄρχιππος (Archippos) is composed of two Greek elements: ἄρχι (archi), which means "first" or "chief," and ἵππος (hippos), which means "horse." It was a common Greek name at the time, found among several figures from antiquity. For Archippus, we do not know of any other family members in the New Testament, although some ancient manuscripts suggest links with the family of Philemon.
G0751.emploi: Archippus appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Pauline epistles written at the same time and possibly addressed to the same region: Colossians and Philemon. Each mention reveals an aspect of his role: first, as a fellow soldier engaged in proclaiming the Gospel, and then, as a servant to whom a particular ministry has been entrusted. Paul seems to have a personal relationship with him and cares about his faithfulness to the mission received. The context of both passages shows that Archippus is a prominent Christian in the local Church, respected by Paul and involved in ministry.
G0751.portee: For the Christian reader, Archippus illustrates the importance of remaining faithful to the ministry one has received from God. Paul's exhortation to "take heed" and "fulfill" this ministry reminds that every believer is responsible for the task entrusted to them, whether small or great. His example also shows that faithfulness requires vigilance and seriousness. Furthermore, being a "fellow soldier" suggests that the Christian life is not solitary: it is fulfilled in communion with other believers, in a common effort for the Gospel.

sens: Officer who directs a synagogue and presides over worship
Man who exercises religious and administrative authority over the local Jewish community
G0752.detail:
1. The synagogue leader is the administrator responsible for a synagogue: he supervises the building, organizes prayers and readings of the Law, and presides over community meetings. Jairus, who comes to plead with Jesus to heal his daughter, is such a leader (Mark 5:22). It was a position of prestige and authority in Jewish life.

2. This title also designates the man who represents religious authority in his community. The synagogue leader in Luke 13:14 protests against the healing that Jesus has just performed on the Sabbath, showing that he ensures respect for the Law. His authority allows him to speak publicly and oppose actions he deems contrary to tradition.
G0752.origine: The Greek word "archisunagôgos" comes from two roots: "archi" (to begin, to be first) which designates the chief or superior, and "sunagôgé" (synagogue, gathering). It literally means "the first of the synagogue," the one who is at the head. It translates the Hebrew "rosh hakkneseth" (the head of the assembly). The same root "archi" is found in other Greek titles such as "archon" (magistrate).
G0752.emploi: This word appears 9 times in the New Testament, only in the first three Gospels and in Acts. It is mostly encountered in Galilee (Mark and Luke) and in Asia Minor (Acts). Jairus in Mark 5:22-38 is the first example: he comes pleading to Jesus. In Luke 13:14, the synagogue leader shows criticism towards Jesus. In Acts 13:15 and 18:8-17, synagogue leaders react to apostolic preaching. The word always designates a local synagogue leader, a figure of religious power in the Jewish community.
G0752.portee: Encountering this word helps to understand the tensions between Jesus and local Jewish authorities. The synagogue leader represents the established order, tradition, and sometimes even opposition to Jesus — but Jairus also shows that a man of power can come to Jesus in humility and faith, which opens the door to grace. This character reminds us that true faith transcends titles and social positions.

sens: One who designs and directs the construction of a building
Figuratively, one who establishes and organizes a work, a community
G0753.detail:
1. The word refers to the master builder who plans and oversees the construction of a building. He is a skilled artisan, an expert in the design and execution of works. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 3:10 to speak of his own apostolic mission.
2. Figuratively, it designates one who lays the foundations of a lasting work and ensures its organization. In Paul's imagery, the spiritual architect has received from God the wisdom and grace to firmly establish the edifice of the Church, while others will continue the construction.
G0753.origine: The Greek word combines "archi" (chief, principal) and "tekton" (worker, carpenter). It literally means "chief craftsman." It translates the Hebrew "harash" (artisan, worker in wood or stone) into Greek. The word denotes recognized know-how, a competence that is both technical and directive.
G0753.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 3:10. Paul refers to himself as the architect who laid the foundation of the Church in Corinth through the proclamation of the Gospel and the establishment of the community. The context develops an image of construction: the apostle reminds that it is God's grace, not his own carnal wisdom, that allows him this foundational role. Each must then build "upon it" according to the quality of his work.
G0753.portee: This word sheds light on the role of authority and responsibility of the apostle Paul, not as a dominator but as a servant of God endowed with a foundational task. It reminds the Christian reader that every lasting spiritual work requires a solid foundation, laid with wisdom and grace. The image also invites a distinction between the role of the founder and that of subsequent builders, each accountable before God for the quality of his contribution.

sens: Supreme head of the tax collectors in a region
Head of a Roman tax administration
G0754.detail:
1. Chief tax collector designates a high-ranking man in the Roman tax administration: he supervises all the tax collectors (the publicans) in a given region. It is a position of great authority and financial power (Luke 19:2 describes him as "a wealthy man"), as he controls the collection of tributes paid to Rome.
2. The word emphasizes an administrative hierarchy: above the simple publicans who collect taxes from the people, there is a chief who is responsible and who reaps considerable profits — which explains why Zacchaeus, the chief tax collector of Jericho, is presented as one of the richest men in the city.
G0754.origine: The Greek word combines "archi-" (which means "chief" or "first") with "telōnēs" (the publican, tax collector). This composition is typical of Greek for designating a hierarchical superior: the chief tax collector is literally the "first-ranking publican." The term reflects the actual administrative structure of the Roman Empire in Judea.
G0754.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 19:2, to designate Zacchaeus in Jericho. Its unique and precise use indicates that it is a specific and recognized administrative title: Zacchaeus is not just a simple tax collector, but the supervisor of the entire tax administration of his region. This title explains both his exceptional wealth and the symbolic importance of his conversion and repentance.
G0754.portee: The encounter between Jesus and Zacchaeus, the chief tax collector, shows that the Gospel reaches even the highest spheres of power and wealth — even those who exploit the people through the tax system can be transformed by grace. It is a call to every reader, regardless of their social position or past guilt, to seek to see Jesus and to open their hearts to Him.

sens: One who directs the service during a meal or feast
Master of ceremonies responsible for the arrangement of tables and food
G0755.detail:
1. In Greco-Roman antiquity, the master of the feast was an important figure: he oversaw the entire organization of the banquet, ensured the arrangement of the couches (the divans where one reclined while eating), the succession of dishes, and the serving of wine. He was the one who tasted the food and drinks before serving them to the guests. At the wedding in Cana, it is the master of the feast who discovers the miracle when he is brought the wine that Jesus has created (John 2:9): unaware of where this wonderful wine comes from, while the servants know the secret, he is struck by it.
2. The word more broadly designates the person responsible for the meal, one who has authority over the service and the servants. It is a position of honor and trust in a wealthy household or during a wedding.
G0755.origine: The Greek word is composed of "archi" (chief, first) and "triklinos" (triclinium, the room with three couches). The starting image is that of the chief presiding over the room where one reclines while eating. The word describes a function typical of the Roman and Greco-Roman world of the New Testament.
G0755.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the account of the wedding at Cana (John 2:8-9). This episode is the only place in the Bible where this character is mentioned. His role in the narrative is decisive: he is the one who identifies the miracle by discovering that the wine created by Jesus is excellent, although he does not know where it comes from. The Segond translates the word once as "master of the feast" (John 2:8) and once as "knew" (John 2:9), the latter occurrence being an erroneous reading of the edition; the character actually appears in both verses.
G0755.portee: This figure of the master of the feast reminds us that Jesus performs his first public miracle in a context of ordinary life and joy: a wedding. The fact that even the master of the banquet discovers the miracle underscores the invisibility of divine action. The miracle transforms not only water into wine but also changes the normal course of a meal by revealing the glory of Jesus to those who see.

sens: To undertake an action, to set it in motion for the first time
To take the lead, to direct or govern
To be the starting point of a succession or order
G0757.detail:
1. To begin means to take action, to cross the threshold that separates inaction from action. This is what the disciples do when they start to pluck heads of grain on the Sabbath (Mark 2:23), or what Jesus does when he begins to preach "Repent" (Matthew 4:17) — each time, a new act begins. The word emphasizes this transition from rest to activity, from silence to speech.
2. To command or govern means to be at the head, to exercise authority. Jesus uses it to describe the leaders of the nations who dominate the peoples (Mark 10:42) — those who begin, who lead the way, who decide. It is an image of power and primacy.
3. To begin with means to be the starting point: repentance will be preached "beginning from Jerusalem" (Luke 24:47), that is to say, starting from there. The word establishes an order, a succession.
G0757.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of "first," of "at the beginning." In Hebrew, it often translates verbs like חָלַל (to begin) or מָשַׁל (to reign, to dominate). The family of the Greek word includes other words for "chief," "power." The basic image is that of the first step, the starting point — the one who begins is naturally the one who opens the way, who takes the lead.
G0757.emploi: The verb appears 86 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and Acts. It has two main meanings: to begin an action (the most frequent), and to reign or command (less often). In the Gospels, the disciples "begin" to pluck heads of grain, to excuse, to weep, to swear — often when Jesus is present or after his command. Jesus himself "begins" to preach, to teach, to get into a boat. In Acts, the Spirit "begins" to act from Pentecost onward. The sense of reigning appears especially in Mark 10:42, where the leaders "command" the nations. The form sometimes changes the meaning: in the middle voice, the verb clearly means "to begin," while in the active voice, it can also mean "to govern." In difficult passages ("to begin to," "to set about"), the Greek uses a construction that may seem strange in French: it is a Hebraism, a Semitic way of speaking that was natural for the Jewish authors of the Gospels.
G0757.portee: For the modern reader, this verb emphasizes that every action has a beginning: that of Jesus (his preaching, his miracles) does not emerge from nothing, but is inscribed in history and time. It reminds us that faith is not passive: it "gets going," it acts, it transforms. When the disciples begin to do something at the command or example of Jesus, it speaks to us — we too are called to begin, to rise up, and to act.

sens: One who exercises authority, who commands
Magistrate or judge responsible for public order
Member of the Sanhedrin or Jewish religious leader
Leader of a synagogue or head of a community
Hostile spiritual power, demon or prince of evil
G0758.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is that of a person in a position of command and authority: someone who directs, decides, and orders. In the Gospel, Jesus presents himself as the supreme "chief" of the heavenly powers (Revelation 1:5), the one who has authority over all.

2. The word also designates civil magistrates and judges, those who administer justice and maintain public order. When Jesus speaks of the "chiefs of the nations" (Matthew 20:25), he refers to these political authorities who govern the peoples.

3. In the Jewish religious context, "chief" can refer to a member of the Sanhedrin, the assembly of 71 elders who governed the Jewish people. Several of these leaders believed in Jesus but did not dare to confess it publicly (John 12:42).

4. A "chief" can also be the head of a synagogue, like Jairus (Luke 8:41), who had authority over the building and its religious services.

5. Finally, the word designates the powers of evil: Satan is called the "chief of the world" (John 12:31), and demons are placed under the authority of the "chief of demons" (Matthew 9:34).
G0758.origine: The Greek word comes from the root "archō," which means "to command, to lead, to be at the head." The basic image is that of someone walking ahead, guiding and dominating. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this word often translates terms like "nasi" (prince) or "sar" (chief, magistrate), words that also refer to a position of power and leadership.
G0758.emploi: The word appears 36 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Acts. In the Synoptics, it first refers to synagogue leaders (Matthew 9:18, Luke 8:41), then to magistrates and judges (Luke 23:35), and finally to members of the Sanhedrin who oppose Jesus (Luke 23:13, John 7:26). John uses the word to speak of the "chiefs" who believe but hide (John 12:42). Acts reserves it for the political and religious authorities who persecute the apostles (Acts 4:26, 23:5). In 1 Corinthians 2:6-8, Paul designates the "chiefs of this age" as the powers hostile to the Gospel. Finally, Pauline theology personifies the powers of evil using this word: the "chief of demons" (Matthew 9:34) and the "chief of the world" (John 12:31, 14:30).
G0758.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus is the true "chief" before whom all other authority bows (Revelation 1:5). It invites the Christian to discern between legitimate authorities (magistrates, religious leaders) and spiritual powers hostile to God. Finally, it shows that even the religious leaders of his time often rejected Jesus out of social fear, which challenges today's believer not to do the same.

sens: Fragrant and precious substance, often in the form of powder or perfume, used to embalm the dead
Spice or scented essence used in burial rituals according to Jewish custom
G0759.detail:
1. An aromate is a powder or perfume made from plants, barks, or aromatic resins. The women who followed Jesus buy it to embalm his body after his crucifixion, which was a respectful and honorable practice. In Luke 23:56, the women prepare it carefully, understanding the importance of the funeral gesture.
2. These aromates are part of the Jewish burial custom: they were applied to the wrapped body to preserve it and pay homage. John 19:40 precisely describes how Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea wrap Jesus' body with strips of cloth and aromates, following the traditional rite.
G0759.origine: The Greek word ἄρωμα comes from a root expressing odor and aroma. It translates the Hebrew בֶּשֶׂם (besem), which designates aromatic substances, spices, and perfumes. This word originally refers to anything that emits a pleasant and precious smell, often imported from distant lands.
G0759.emploi: The word "aromate" appears four times in the New Testament, only in the accounts of the passion and resurrection of Jesus (Mark, Luke, and John). It always describes the same context: the women who buy or prepare aromates to honor the body of Jesus after his death. Mark 16:1 shows them buying these precious substances; Luke 23:56 and 24:1 describe them preparing and bringing the aromates to the tomb; John 19:40 indicates how Nicodemus uses them during the burial. The word retains its concrete and ritual meaning throughout.
G0759.portee: For the believer, this detail shows the love and respect that the disciples, especially the women, had for Jesus, even after his death. They performed the funeral rites with care, which testifies to their attachment and reverence. This humble and costly gesture reminds us that the honor given to Christ is never lost, even when it seems absurd in the eyes of the world.

sens: king of Judah, son of Abijah and father of Jehoshaphat
G0760.detail: 1. Asa is a king of Judah who appears in the genealogy of Jesus presented by Matthew. He is the son of Abijah and the father of Jehoshaphat, holding an important place in the Davidic lineage that leads to Jesus Christ (Matthew 1:7-8). Although Matthew does not report any details of his reign, his presence in this genealogy underscores the continuity of God's plan through the royal generations of Judah.
G0760.origine: The name Asa comes from the Hebrew אָסַף (asaph), which means "to gather" or "to collect." This name was borne by several important figures in the Old Testament, notably by a leader of the Temple musicians. In the context of Matthew's genealogy, it refers to the historical king of Judah also known in the accounts of the Old Testament.
G0760.emploi: Asa appears twice in the New Testament, only in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1:7-8. Matthew mentions him as an essential link in the genealogical chain connecting Solomon to Jesus, thus establishing that Jesus descends from the royal lineage of David. Although the synoptic gospels do not report any events concerning his life, his presence in this passage shows the importance that Matthew attaches to demonstrating that Jesus is the promised Messiah, heir to the throne of David.
G0760.portee: For the Christian reader, Asa represents a link in the unbroken chain of divine providence. His presence in the genealogy of Jesus affirms that even the kings of Judah, despite their weaknesses and failures, participated in God's design in preparing for the coming of the Messiah. This encourages the believer to see God's hand at work throughout history, generation after generation, to fulfill His promises.

sens: that cannot be shaken or moved
that cannot be overturned or destroyed
that is firm and stable over time
that withstands all shocks and threats
G0761.detail:
1. In a literal and concrete sense, the word designates something fixed and immobile, which does not move under the effect of an external force. When Paul's ship runs aground near Malta, the bow remains "immobile" stuck in the sand, while the stern breaks under the violence of the waves (Acts 27:41): this is a material solidity, unshakeable in the face of the storm's assaults.

2. In a figurative and spiritual sense, the word describes what is stable, durable, and indestructible, particularly in matters of faith and eternal kingdom. When the Kingdom received by believers is described as "unshakeable" (Hebrews 12:28), it means that it can never be lost, overturned, or annihilated, unlike earthly things that pass away: it is a promise of permanence and ultimate victory.
G0761.origine: The word is formed from the negative particle "a-" (which means "not") and the verb "saleuo" (to shake, to agitate, to waver). The basic image is that of something that cannot be shaken, which remains firm in the face of tremors. It is a compound word that emphasizes the impossibility of movement or instability. In Exodus and Deuteronomy, Hebrew words designate what is firmly attached or fixed.
G0761.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, in two distinct contexts. First in Acts 27:41, it literally qualifies the bow of the ship that has run aground, which is firmly embedded in the sand and does not move despite the waves. Then in Hebrews 12:28, it takes on a theological significance: the Kingdom of God received by believers is described as unshakeable, to encourage the recipients to persevere in worship and recognition of God. The same word thus transitions from a physical reality to a spiritual reality.
G0761.portee: This word invites the believer to base their life on eternal and indestructible realities, not on earthly goods or securities that waver. In particular, Hebrews 12:28 strengthens confidence: if the Kingdom received from God is unshakeable, no storm of this world can tear it away. It is a call to build one's faith on the immovable rock of God's promise.

sens: that cannot be extinguished, that burns without stopping
that never ceases, that lasts forever
in a figurative sense: a punishment or eternal chastisement from which one cannot escape
G0762.detail:
1. The word first describes a material fire that cannot be extinguished once it has been lit. John the Baptist speaks of the unquenchable fire in which Jesus will burn the chaff at judgment (Matthew 3:12; Luke 3:17): it is an image of total and definitive destruction.
2. The idea expands to anything that cannot end or disappear. An "inextinguishable" punishment never stops; it cannot be halted or annulled, unlike an ordinary fire that can be extinguished with water.
3. In Jesus' words about hell (Mark 9:43, 9:45), the "inextinguishable fire" symbolizes eternal judgment: it is no longer just a fire that burns for a long time, but a punishment that persists forever in the world to come.
G0762.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "to extinguish." The prefix "a-" at the beginning means "not" or "without," so the whole word literally means "that cannot be extinguished." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, a similar expression ("fire that does not go out") is found in passages about divine judgment, notably in Job 20:26.
G0762.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always to describe a fire. John the Baptist uses it in his preaching of repentance (Matthew 3:12; Luke 3:17) to warn that the Messiah will judge the unrepentant in a fire that cannot be extinguished. Jesus takes up this expression when speaking of hell (Mark 9:43, 9:45), threatening those who cause little ones to stumble. The context is always that of final judgment and the separation between the righteous and the unjust. The word does not appear anywhere to describe an ordinary or useful fire.
G0762.portee: This image of the inextinguishable fire emphasizes the seriousness of divine judgment and the impossibility of escaping or negotiating it. It calls believers to take the warning of repentance seriously and not to assume that they can live without consequences. At the same time, it underscores that salvation in Jesus is a matter of urgency: one cannot postpone the decision to turn to Him.

sens: Absence of fear or respect toward God
State or behavior contrary to piety
Acts or words that offend God
Worldly desires and cravings distant from God
G0763.detail:
1. Impiety is the absence of fear or respect toward God, a culpable indifference to His holiness and authority. This is what Paul refers to in Romans 1:18 when he speaks of the wrath of God revealed against all impiety of men.
2. It is a moral and spiritual state contrary to piety: one who lives in impiety refuses to turn to God and rejects His will. The grace of God teaches to renounce impiety (Titus 2:12) and to live differently.
3. Impiety manifests itself through concrete acts and injurious words: Jude 1:15 speaks of the acts of impiety committed by the ungodly, true works that oppose God.
4. It encompasses worldly cravings and desires contrary to God: in Jude 1:18, impious cravings refer to those carnal desires that distance one from the Lord and despise Him.
G0763.origine: The word comes from the Greek asebès (impious), itself formed from the root sebô (to fear, to revere) with the negation a- at the beginning. Asebeia thus literally means the absence of reverential fear toward God. It is a word from the same family as asebès (impious, without piety) and sebeia (piety, reverence). In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew words that denote rebellion and wickedness before God.
G0763.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, concentrated in the doctrinal epistles and in Jude. In Romans 1:18 and 11:26, Paul speaks of it as a spiritual reality against which the wrath of God is exercised and from which Christ frees Israel. In 2 Timothy 2:16, impiety is the fatal fruit of vain and profane discourse that eats away like gangrene. Titus 2:12 presents it as something to be rejected, thanks to the grace of God. In the epistle of Jude, impiety characterizes false teachers: it is their acts (1:15) and their desires (1:18) that mark them. The word always denotes an active or passive opposition to God, never a mere weakness.
G0763.portee: Impiety is not an innocent mistake or a forgivable ignorance: it is a culpable refusal of God that provokes His wrath. For the believer, understanding this word prompts him to examine his heart: does he push God away through worldly desires or through indifference? The Good News is that the grace of God teaches precisely to abandon impiety (Titus 2:12): the Christian can change, not by his own strength, but by allowing himself to be transformed by this grace.

sens: To commit acts contrary to the will of God, without fear or respect for Him
To live in a profane manner, far from any obedience to God
G0764.detail: 1. The word designates the concrete action of committing acts of impiety — acts that offend God by despising His law and authority. In Jude 1:15, it speaks of all the acts of impiety that sinners have committed: it is the totality of transgressions, injurious words, and insolences against God. 2. More broadly, it is a way of living, a habitual behavior marked by the absence of fear of God and the refusal of His lordship — the opposite of piety, which is respect and obedience toward the Lord.
G0764.origine: The word comes from ἀ- (negation: "not") and σεβέω ("to venerate, to respect"). It thus literally designates one who does not venerate, who does not honor God. It is a term that directly opposes piety — the reverential fear and obedience toward the Lord. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates Hebrew words for "rebellion" or "wickedness," showing that impiety is primarily a rebellion against God.
G0764.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in the letter of Jude. Jude uses it in a passage recalling God's judgments on those who act without piety: he enumerates impious acts (transgressions of the law, injurious words) to show that God will hold all sinners accountable. The context is that of the final judgment and the warning addressed to Christians against false teachers and the misguided who lead a profane life.
G0764.portee: This word invites the believer to take seriously what God judges as impiety. Not only great crimes, but every act, every word contrary to divine will counts before Him and will be judged. It is a call to reverential fear of God and to live in obedience, knowing that there is a judgment awaiting those who act with impiety.

sens: One who despises God, who refuses to revere Him and obey Him
One who lives without fear or respect for God
One who opposes the justice and holiness of God
G0765.detail:
1. The impious is someone who rejects God and does not fear Him: he does not give Him the honor and obedience that are due. This is the opposite of one who fears and worships God. Romans 5:6 speaks of Christ dying "for the ungodly," that is, for those who lived in this contempt for God.
2. The impious is one who lives without religion, without respect for the divine: he acts as if God did not exist or did not matter. In 1 Peter 4:18, the question "what will become of the ungodly?" shows that he is doomed to judgment.
3. The impious actively opposes righteousness and holiness: he is ranked alongside sinners, the wicked, and rebels (1 Timothy 1:9), and even murderers and parricides. In 2 Peter 2:5-6, the ungodly of Noah's time and the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah illustrate those who provoked God's wrath by their refusal to obey His justice.
G0765.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek σέβω (sebô), which means "to revere," "to honor," "to worship." The negative prefix ἀ- (a-) means "without": the impious is thus literally one who is "without reverence," who does not worship God. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew רָשַׁע (rasha), the wicked, one who willfully transgresses the will of God. It is a strong moral term, designating not ignorance, but the active refusal to fear and serve God.
G0765.emploi: This word appears 9 times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles of Paul, Peter, and Jude. It describes the enemies of God and the righteous, and those who will be judged. In Romans 4:5 and 5:6, Paul uses it to show that Christ justifies precisely those who are "ungodly" — this is the power of grace. In 1 Timothy 1:9, it appears in a list of moral categories showing against whom the law is directed. In 2 Peter 2 and Jude, the term appears in warnings against false teachers and destroyers who will be punished as the ungodly of Sodom and the flood were. It is a word of judgment: it marks those who refuse God and will be condemned.
G0765.portee: This word reminds the Christian that the ungodly — one who refuses to fear and honor God — is exactly the one for whom Christ died. The grace of God is not primarily directed at the virtuous, but at those who live in contempt of God. At the same time, Jude and Peter show that impiety has consequences: it provokes judgment. The believer will draw a double lesson from this: on one hand, humility before the mercy received; on the other, vigilance against anything in him that would stray from the fear of God.

sens: Total absence of restraint in carnal and sensual pleasures
Moral disorder that rejects all limits and respect for others
Excess and debauchery delivered without shame or guilt
Dishonorable conduct that abandons all dignity and modesty
G0766.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes unrestrained debauchery in bodily pleasures: lust, excess in eating and drinking, frenzied pursuit of sensations. It is a complete surrender to what carnal desire demands, without restraint. In Ephesians 4:19, it is seen coupled with impurity and greed: these people "have given themselves over to dissolution, to work all uncleanness with greediness."
2. In a broader sense, it is a moral disorder that refuses any limits, any shame, any respect. In Galatians 5:19, Paul lists it among the works of the flesh, its carnal manifestations. It opposes the self-discipline of the Christian who wants to honor his body as a temple of the Holy Spirit.
3. It is also the insolence of the debauched who display themselves without modesty. In 1 Peter 4:3, the apostle mentions those who "have accomplished the will of the Gentiles, walking in dissolution, lusts, excess of wine." It is an entire lifestyle of degradation.
4. It particularly characterizes one who persists in evil: in 2 Peter 2:7, the righteous Lot "was distressed by the conduct of those men given to dissolution." This dissolution becomes a hallmark of a life turned away from divine justice.
G0766.origine: The Greek word comes from ἀσελγής, which means "unrestrained, shameless." It carries the idea of an absence (the prefix ἀ-) of any measure or modesty. It is a word often applied to bodily debauchery, notably to the scandals of the flesh. The root evokes one who crosses boundaries, who fears neither God nor the gaze of men. It is a strong term that does not describe a mere error, but a voluntary surrender to impurity.
G0766.emploi: The word appears ten times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and the Catholic epistles. Paul enumerates it among the sins of the flesh (Galatians 5:19, Ephesians 4:19), and warns the Christian who has left it (Romans 13:13). In 2 Corinthians 12:21, it is a serious offense in Corinth. In 1 Peter 4:3, it refers to the rebellious past of the new Christian. In 2 Peter 2, it marks the false teachers who will lose judgment, and in Jude, it arises among the heretics who corrupt the Church. The context is always one of warning and rejection: it is a capital sin that manifests a heart far from God.
G0766.portee: This word reminds the Christian that his body is not a playground for passions. The Gospel calls for a purity of heart that rejects debauchery and honors the temple of the Holy Spirit. Seeing that this sin is cited alongside false prophets and renegades should alert us: moral dissolution is often a sign of a soul that has betrayed its relationship with God. It is a call to vigilance and self-control.

sens: that has no mark or distinguishing sign
that is obscure, unknown, without prestige
G0767.detail:
1. The word literally denotes that which has no mark or sign that distinguishes it: an uncircumcised child, for example, did not have this mark that characterized the Jews (Genesis 30:42 in the Greek Old Testament). It is the absence of what would make it visible, recognizable, important.

2. Figuratively, the word describes something obscure, unknown, without social prestige or importance. In Acts 21:39, Paul, when introducing himself as a citizen of Tarsus, emphasizes that it is a city "that is not without importance"—in other words, not an ordinary or obscure city. The negative expression ("not without importance") is a polite way of saying that it enjoys a certain reputation.
G0767.origine: The word comes from the root σῆμα (sêma), which means "mark" or "sign." A word is formed by adding the privative prefix ἀ-, which means "without." Thus ἄσημος literally means "without mark." The original image is that of an object or person devoid of the sign that would identify or value it: an uncircumcised child was considered without the distinguishing sign of the people of God.
G0767.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 21:39, where Paul speaks of Tarsus. Although the text says "a city that is not without importance" (negative turn), the Greek adjective ἄσημος fundamentally means "without importance" or "obscure." Paul uses it here to defend the reputation of his hometown: by denying that it is ἄσημος, he asserts that it is known and esteemed. This ironic or polite turn was common to express the opposite.
G0767.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on what gives value and importance: not visible marks, not fame or human prestige, but the relationship with God. Paul defends Tarsus out of natural pride, but for the Christian, it is an opportunity to remember that what truly matters is never social importance or worldly renown.

sens: One of the twelve tribes of Israel, descended from Jacob's son of that name
The descendants and territory assigned to this tribe in the promised land
A member of this tribe
G0768.detail: 1. Aser is a tribe of Israel founded by Aser, the son of Jacob (Genesis 30:13). In Luke 2:36, Anna, the prophetess who recognizes Jesus in the Temple, is explicitly identified as "of the tribe of Aser," showing that she belongs to this lineage. 2. Upon entering Canaan, Aser received a territory in the northwest of the promised land. In Revelation 7:6, the tribe of Aser is listed among the twelve tribes whose members are sealed during John's eschatological vision, showing that even dispersed, it remains identifiable in God's plan. 3. Each person from this tribe carries the identity of Aser: this is the case with Anna, who remains faithful to worship in Jerusalem despite trials.
G0768.origine: The name "Aser" comes from the Hebrew אָשֵׁר (Ašēr) which means "happy" or "blessed." Rachel, in naming her son (born of a maidservant), said: "For my happiness!" (Genesis 30:13). The tribe thus bears the name of the founding son of this lineage.
G0768.emploi: Aser appears only twice in the provided Greek New Testament. In Luke 2:36, it refers to the tribe from which Anna originates, a devout woman who awaited the redemption of Israel and recognizes the child Messiah. In Revelation 7:6, Aser is listed in the solemn enumeration of the twelve tribes whose 12,000 members are sealed in a vision of eschatological salvation. These two uses emphasize continuity: despite the historical dispersion of the tribes after exile, God recognizes and seals a remnant of Aser.
G0768.portee: For the Christian reader, the presence of Anna from the tribe of Aser shows that God does not abandon His dispersed people: a faithful woman, long forgotten, remains vigilant and recognizes the Savior. In Revelation, the mention of Aser among the sealed tribes affirms that salvation forgets no one and that the heritage of Israel persists in God's eternal plan.

sens: State of lacking physical strength, vigor, or health
Lack of moral strength, courage, or firmness
State of limitation or powerlessness in the face of circumstances
Human condition exposed and vulnerable before God
G0769G.detail:
1. Physical or bodily weakness: this is the lack of strength in the body, its natural fragility. Paul mentions his own physical weakness upon arriving in Corinth (1 Corinthians 2:3), and Jesus heals a woman bent over by an "infirmity" for eighteen years (Luke 13:11-12).

2. Moral or spiritual weakness: this is the lack of firmness in the face of temptations or difficulties. When Paul says, "I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh" (Romans 6:19), he refers to the Christians' inability to turn away from sin on their own.

3. Powerlessness or limitation: this is the inability to accomplish something by one's own strength. The Holy Spirit Himself intercedes for us "for we do not know what we ought to pray for" (Romans 8:26) — we are limited in our resources.

4. The vulnerable condition of man before God: recognizing one's weakness is acknowledging that one is entirely dependent on God. Paul boasts of his weaknesses so that "the power of Christ may rest upon me" (2 Corinthians 12:9) — our fragility becomes the place where divine grace acts.
G0769G.origine: The word comes from the adjective "asthénès" (ἀσθενής) which means "without strength." It is composed of the negative prefix "a-" and a root related to vigor. It is a common term in Greek to describe the absence of power, whether physical, moral, or spiritual. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew "kashál" (כָּשַׁל), which means "to stumble" or "to be overwhelmed" — the idea of a person who cannot stand on their own.
G0769G.emploi: This word appears fourteen times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul. It primarily refers to physical weaknesses: illnesses and infirmities (Luke 5:15, 1 Corinthians 15:43). But Paul uses it well beyond that: the weakness of the body in Corinth (1 Corinthians 2:3), that of the flesh in the struggle against sin (Romans 6:19), and spiritual impotence in the face of the challenges of prayer (Romans 8:26). There is a remarkable progression: Paul acknowledges his personal weakness, then transforms it into a reason for glory, since "the power of [God] is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). The letter to the Hebrews uses it to show that Jesus, the perfect high priest, "can sympathize with our weaknesses" (Hebrews 4:15) — His compassion is nourished by His own experience of human temptation.
G0769G.portee: This word profoundly changes our relationship to our own insufficiency. Far from being an obstacle to the Christian life, weakness becomes the point of encounter with God. It teaches us humility, detaches us from self-sufficiency, and opens us to grace. It is a call to stop relying on our own strength and to fully trust in the One whose power is infinite. Jesus sympathizes with our weaknesses: He does not judge us for them, but understands them — which brings peace and restoration.

sens: State of physical weakness, bodily illness
Incapacity or lasting functional limitation
Spiritual or moral suffering, insufficiency of being
Human condition of fragility and limitation
G0769H.detail:
1. Infirmity primarily refers to a physical illness or ailment that weakens the body: the bent woman in Luke 13:11 suffered from an infirmity for eighteen years that prevented her from standing up, and Jesus frees her from this affliction (Luke 13:12).
2. The word also describes the state of a person severely affected: the man in John 5:5 had been ill for thirty-eight years, reduced to powerlessness by his condition.
3. Infirmity can be spiritual or moral: in Romans 8:26, it is the insufficiency of our human nature that prevents us from praying properly, which the Holy Spirit comes to assist.
4. The term finally evokes the fundamental fragility of humanity: in Hebrews 5:2, the high priest must sympathize with our infirmities because he himself shares this condition of weakness.
G0769H.origine: The Greek word comes from "asthénès" which means "without strength, weak." The basic image is that of the absence of vigor or power. In Hebrew, words like "kashál" (falling, stumbling) or other terms denoting weakness are translated by this word in the Greek Old Testament. The family of Greek words related to "asthéneia" includes the adjective "asthénès" and the verb "asthenéô" (to be weak, ill).
G0769H.emploi: The word appears nine times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and in Paul's epistles. In the Gospels (Matthew, Luke, John), it primarily refers to physical illnesses that Jesus heals: the infirmities from which people are freed, the diseases from which women are healed (Luke 5:15, 8:2). In Paul, the meaning broadens: he speaks of his own infirmities (2 Corinthians 12:9-10), but also of the infirmity of our nature that cannot pray as it should (Romans 8:26). In Hebrews, infirmity becomes a condition shared by all human beings, a common point of compassion (Hebrews 5:2). The plural "infirmities" emphasizes the multiplicity of forms of this weakness.
G0769H.portee: This word reminds the Christian that weakness is not a shame but a human reality. Jesus did not despise the infirm; He healed them with compassion, showing that God takes our suffering seriously. For Paul, recognizing his infirmity paradoxically becomes an opportunity to discover the strength of Christ, which is fully manifested in our fragility. This word invites us not to idolize strength or health, but to receive God's grace in our condition as limited creatures.

sens: to lack physical strength, to be sick
to lack moral or spiritual vigor
to lack conviction, to hesitate in one's faith
G0770G.detail:
1. The most direct meaning is that of physical weakness, of being sick: to be afflicted in one's body, incapable of physical effort. This is the state of the sick person who is so ill that one cannot see them (John 5:3), or the state Paul refers to when he delights "in weaknesses" in the sense of his infirmities (2 Corinthians 12:10).
2. Weakness can also refer to a moral or spiritual incapacity, a lack of inner vigor. Romans 8:3 speaks of the flesh that sin renders "weak" — it cannot accomplish the will of God. Similarly, a believer can be "weak" in their religious conviction, like the one who "only eats vegetables" out of scruple (Romans 14:2): they do not have the firm confidence that others possess.
3. A more nuanced meaning appears when the word designates one who hesitates, who lacks certainty in matters of faith. This is why Paul can say: "when I am weak, then I am strong" (2 Corinthians 12:10) — he acknowledges his human limitations and relies on the strength of Christ, which paradoxically makes him spiritually stronger.
G0770G.origine: The word comes from the adjective ἀσθενής ("weak"), formed with the negative prefix ἀ- and a root meaning "strength." The verb thus expresses the state or action of being in weakness. In classical and biblical Greek, it opposes strength and vigor. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it often renders the Hebrew כָּשַׁל (kashal), which primarily means to stumble, then to fail or be brought low, an image that reinforces the idea of loss of capacity.
G0770G.emploi: This verb appears about fifteen times in the New Testament, especially in Paul and in the Gospel of John. In the Gospels, it often designates physical illness: Matthew, Luke, and John use it to speak of those who are sick and whom Jesus heals or visits. In Paul, the word takes on a moral and theological significance: he uses it to describe the weakness of the flesh that cannot obey God (Romans 8:3), or to refer to the scruples of novice believers regarding food offered to idols (Romans 14:2). In the letters to the Corinthians, Paul speaks of his own "weakness" (2 Corinthians 11:21, 12:10) in contrast to the pride of false apostles, and he even presents it as a place where the power of Christ is exercised. The word can designate either the state of one who is weak or the action of weakening, of becoming weak.
G0770G.portee: This word invites the Christian to a clear honesty about their limits. Paul does not hide his weaknesses or those of young converts; he acknowledges them as real and sometimes inevitable. The teaching reveals that human weakness is not a sin, but a condition that God knows and accepts: it is in it that His strength can be displayed. For the reader, this is a comfort: being weak is not disqualifying; it is recognizing one's dependence on God.

sens: to suffer from a physical infirmity, from a disease of the body
to be weak, without strength
to lack moral firmness or conviction in faith
G0770H.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to be afflicted with a disease, to suffer from an infirmity that weakens the body. This is seen in all the healing accounts: the son of the royal official was sick in Capernaum (John 4:46), Lazarus was sick and died (John 11:1-3), and the apostles went everywhere healing the sick (Matthew 10:8).
2. In a broader sense, the word designates weakness itself, the state of one who does not have the strength to function normally, whether physically or morally. This is why one can say of a person that they "are sick" without having the flu: they lack vitality, capacity.
3. In Paul's epistles in particular, the word takes on a spiritual and moral significance: having weak faith, lacking conviction, being unstable in one's beliefs or practices. Thus Paul speaks of "the one who is weak in faith" (Romans 14:1), showing that weakness can also be that of spiritual certainty.
G0770H.origine: The Greek word ἀσθενέω comes from ἀσθενής, which literally means "without strength." It is composed of the privative α- ("without") and the root σθένος (strength). In ancient Hebrew, the main word it translates is כָּשַׁל, which means "to stumble, to fail, to collapse." This image of weakness that causes one to wobble or fall is at the heart of the word: it is the absence of the necessary strength to stand, both literally and figuratively.
G0770H.emploi: The verb appears about twenty times in the New Testament. In the four Gospels, it is mainly used to describe the sick whom Jesus heals: the centurion's servant, the crowds who came to touch him, Lazarus. In Acts, it describes the state of the sick brought to the apostles to be healed. In Paul, the word is enriched: it designates not only physical illness (2 Timothy 4:20), but also spiritual weakness — that of the believer who doubts, who lacks moral strength or conviction (Romans 4:19, 14:1-2). In 2 Corinthians 11-13, Paul uses it several times to express human weakness in the face of God's power. It is a word of concrete and existential experience.
G0770H.portee: For the Christian reader, this word opens two essential reflections. First, it reminds us that Jesus and his disciples were given the mission to heal the sick (Matthew 10:8): illness is not ignored; it is at the heart of the Church's commitment. Secondly, the use of the word by Paul invites us to recognize weakness — not as a shame, but as a human reality where God acts. Physical or moral weakness does not distance one from God; it can even become the place where His strength is manifested (2 Corinthians 12:10).

sens: the state of one who lacks physical or moral strength
the inability to accomplish something without help
a personal flaw or limitation
G0771.detail: 1. The word primarily designates a weakness or lack of strength — physical or moral — in a person. Paul speaks of the "weaknesses" of those who are not strong, that is, those who have little assurance or few resources (Romans 15:1). 2.
